📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Season 35 of Dancing With the Stars marks Alfonso Ribeiro’s fifth season hosting the show, and he has no idea how it will end.

According to recent reports, after winning season 19 with Witney Carson, The Fresh Prince of Bel-Air joined the series as a co-host in its 31st season, a year that he believes laid the foundation for the show’s resurgence. “I think we owe a debt of gratitude to Charli D’Amelio doing the show. … Her being literally one of the most popular social media TikTok stars opened the door to an audience that previously didn’t care about this show,” he tells The Hollywood Reporter of what he pinpoints to DWTS’ spike in popularity (and ratings) in recent years. Related Stories TV 'The Secret Lives of Mormon Wives: Orange County' Renewed at Hulu TV Lindsay Hubbard Teases 'Summer House' Spinoff 'In the City' Season 2: "Better Than Season One".

The TikTok star certainly brought latest eyes to the series, but Ribeiro also refreshed it as host. After one year executing the job alongside Tyra Banks, Julianne Hough stepped in as his co-host, and the duo have remained at the post since. They both bring unique perspectives to DWTS: Ribeiro, as a celebrity who won the series, and Hough, as a former professional dancer and judge.

Recent findings suggest that ribeiro notes there’s so many things that he loves about hosting the show, but one standout is the mentorship he’s able to offer the celebrities. This year, his Fresh Prince sister Tatyana Ali hit the ballroom floor, which he says has been “beautiful for me to experience with her.”.

Ali is one of five couples still competing for a chance to win the Len Goodman mirrorball trophy on Tuesday night. Ribeiro admittedly doesn’t know what factors will hold more weight when determining this year’s winner.

“It is quite wild to me because this is a very different season than any other season we’ve ever had,” he notes. “So, all of the normal things that we would be able to gauge doesn’t really exist this year.”.

One thing Ribeiro hopes is that the portion of the audience spreading hate towards contestants will fade in future seasons. “At the end of the day, this is a dance competition show. This isn’t life or death. No one’s life is changing that greatly from this. It is designed for people to let loose, have some fun and truly enjoy these incredible celebrities,” he adds.

To commemorate the finale of DWTS, Ribeiro chats with THR below about the ups-and-downs of season 35; being in the ballroom and getting the chance to dance with Ali; his opinion on fans who believe celebrities with prior dance experience shouldn’t be cast on the show; and why you won’t ever see him compete on another All-Star (or all-winners) iteration of DWTS.

How does it feel to almost be at the finish line of season 35 of Dancing With the Stars?

In a recent development, this is an incredibly epic season. The numbers, the fans and the interest has been through the roof. We feel really blessed to do something no other show has really ever done in history, which is come back from the brink of extinction to turn around and become the No. 1 show on television. We’ve got a great cast, and they’ve done an incredible job of opening themselves up and allowing America to get to know them. Deena Katz and Conrad Green put a great team together.

The season 35 finale is going to be airing live coast-to-coast for the first time. What do you think that indicates about the growth and reach of the show that this was so wanted by fans, but also so much so that the affiliates came to an agreement for this to happen?

That’s a major move, right? The only thing on television that does that are sporting events, and the fact that we can move side by side with the NFL and NBA, and people are willing to, on a Tuesday night on the West Coast and Mountain time, come home a little early so that they could watch the show live is quite spectacular when you really think of it. That the affiliates and the network have that much trust in doing this as a finale claims that they truly believe that this will work out great for the show and for the sponsors and the companies buying ad time. It says a lot about what they believe in the show.

Do you think that airing the finale live could be a potential test to see how the viewership comes in to see if the show would adapt this live format for a future season?

I can’t really speak on it, obviously, because I don’t know anyone’s thoughts. Anything I say would be conjecture, not anything real. I actually believe that it works the way that it works so far. Of course, we’d love for everyone on the West Coast and everyone in the Mountain time zone to be able to vote for their favorites. I think the interesting way would be to do it on Disney+ and not necessarily on ABC. But the question becomes, does the audience truly support it? And if the audience supports it, then why not, right?

If the numbers end up being as good or better, then of course let’s do it. But there are things that would severely be hampered by that. Technically speaking, ABC News Tonight is the No. 1 broadcast show on Tuesday nights, so you’d be giving up on that for the success of Dancing. The smarter people will make that decision, and we’ll see where that leads us. We’re super excited that we’re getting to experience this particular case. Hopefully all of America and everybody on the West Coast watches it live and we break ratings and voting records.

Sources indicate that tatyana has had such an incredible journey. What has it been like being able to be there and be a part of that journey?

I’ve been trying to get her to do the show for many years, and the timing just wasn’t right. And so happy she did, and really, mostly, so happy for her. It isn’t about me; it’s about her and what she is getting to experience. The little girl I met in 1990, [she’s] all grown up. She’s such a special person. What this show did for me was show America who Alfonso really was, not that character [from Fresh Prince]; same situation for her: getting to experience who Tatyana Ali is and people falling in love with the beautiful human she is.

What was your reaction when she came to you with the idea for you to be a part of her Dedication Night dance in honor of James [Avery]?

It started obviously with the producers asking me the question first. When we finally talked about it, it was already a yes. I expressed my very small concerns of, does that make it look like I’m favoring someone over everyone else, and will that be something that we ultimately have to deal with? And everyone came to the conclusion that that wouldn’t be an problem. The thing that took it over the top for me was that the dedication was to James Avery, and it was bigger than just this show. James Avery played my dad on three different shows, so dedicating it to him felt so right. It was a great opportunity for us to spend extra time together and go through the process of doing a competitive number on the show. I dance all the time on the show, but to be part of a competitive number made it extra special.

You have seen the growth the show has had in the past few years. What do you think it has been about these past two seasons that have really hooked a wider audience and opened the show up to more people?

In a recent development, I actually think it goes back further than the last two seasons. I think we owe a debt of gratitude to Charli D’Amelio for doing the show. Before her season, it was always an older audience. It wasn’t what it is today, and I think that her being literally one of the most popular social media TikTok stars opened the door to an audience that previously didn’t care about this show and always looked at it as, Oh, that’s my grandmother’s show. That’s my parents’ show. It wasn’t their show, and I think Charli D’Amelio made it OK for it to be their show. As the years went along, it just grew and grew, and more people talked about it, and it became this very cool energy that moved through the younger generation. Back in the day, we used to have this term, the “water cooler” TV demonstrates, where people would stand around the water cooler at the office and talk about the show. Well, social media has become the water cooler, and this show has gained on that.

It has been revealed that it’s beautiful to watch how the young audience is falling in love with the show. I certainly do hope that the younger audience can be fickle, and know as quickly as they fall in love with something, they fall out of love with it. I’m hoping that they stay in love with it for a while, and recognize that what we’re trying to do is bring love and joy to an audience. I will say that the audience out there that adds a lot of hate, negativity and bullying — I hope that goes away and it becomes more of just love and joy. At the end of the day, this is a dance competition show. This isn’t life or death. No one’s life is changing that greatly from this. It is designed for people to let loose, have some fun and truly enjoy these incredible celebrities.

In a recent development, there has been a lot of chatter and conversation online this season. Has there been one specific conversation online that has specifically stood out to you?

No, I’m not going to say anything specific. What I will say is everyone is entitled to their perspective of what they think the show is, and I would say that for me, it isn’t necessarily a show about people who have no dance experience learning to dance. You do that in Hollywood, it becomes a really short list of people. I look at this show as this is just a bunch of celebrities coming together to learn ballroom dancing. Whether they start with a lot of experience or they start with zero experience, it’s about the journey that they all go on.

What is your favorite part about hosting Dancing With the Stars?

Recent findings suggest that I really do love being almost a mentor to a lot of our celebrities. I go in on Monday and I’m there all day watching every one of the performances and being there as a support system; I’m there for all of it. I’ve been the host of the show, [this year] being my fifth season, and yes, I was a contestant, but I was also a fan from season one on, so I’ve watched almost every person that’s ever done this show in all 35 seasons. That’s really the part that I enjoy: I enjoy being there for them, and it’s a gift that I get to be a part of their journey in some form.

Do you have a favorite number you performed on the show?

Recent findings suggest that my favorite was my Paso Doble to “Turn Down for What.” That was my all-time favorite one. It was a lot of fun to do that. I mean, the music — songs make dances, and you would never think [of doing] a Paso Doble to that song, but yet Witney choreographed a great number having Lindsay [Arnold] on it with us.

Recent findings suggest that viewers always talk about how they want a potential second all-star season, but something I have always wondered about is an all-winners. If they ever did that and the idea was floated by you, is there any world where you would ever consider doing an all-winners season?

It has been revealed that no, and that’s mostly because of the fact that I am the host of the show, and I certainly wouldn’t be giving that job to someone else while I dance again. The answer would be no. You know, we always talk about the all-star season. We always talk about how much fun that would be. The only problem with an all-star season, and especially now, think about how many of our fresh fans dislike the idea that they have dancers [competing on the show] that are really good dancers. So, you’d literally be making a show that all of those audience members wouldn’t ultimately want to watch. [It’d be] fun for the people doing it, right? But is it fun for that new audience that loves the idea of it being people who couldn’t dance in the beginning?

Industry observers note that I think the two fan favorites from this season so far are Connor [Wood] and Tatyana. Tatyana, if she was to win, will be the lowest scoring winner in the history of the show on week one.

It has been revealed that that’s this new audience. Tatyana doesn’t make the finale 10 years ago with that audience, because it was never about that. Now you have audience members that really want to see the Guillermos. They want to see the Tatyanas and the Connors and, going back to last season, the Andy Richters. They want to see those people go a long way because, at the end of the day, most of our audience can’t dance, so they’re excited about watching someone who reminds them of themselves achieve something that they would love to do.

I don’t know if I win if I’m on a season now, even though I’m not a trained dancer. Just the idea that I have dance experience, this audience is harder on those people, and I think that’s wrong, personally. That’s my own personal [opinion], not from the show’s perspective. I think it’s wrong because I think if we had 16 people on the show in the beginning who couldn’t dance, I don’t know if that’s an enjoyable show to watch.

I think watching some really great dances, some dances that are mediocre and dances that are not so good, I don’t think that the show would be as successful. I question that audience because I go, man, I think you kind of want your Jenna Dewan’s and your Harry [Shum Jr.]’s and your Charli D’Amelio’s, right? You you want those people on there, and you want to see them continue to get better.

Who do you think will be joining you in the Dancing With the Stars winner’s circle Tuesday night?

Not a clue. I really don’t know. It is quite wild to me because this is a very different season than any other season we’ve ever had. So, all of the normal things that we would be able to gauge doesn’t really exist this year. A lot of people online say that Connor’s getting the most votes, right? OK, but he’s also the lowest-scoring celebrity. So where does that fit? How does that work? How does the scoring system work? All of those questions leave us to, you know, if you were to look at scores through the season so far, Amber [Glenn] and Pasha [Pashkov] and Ezra [Frech] and Daniella [Karagach] are your hands down two of your favorites. Well, we don’t know where they are on the list, so I have no clue. I really don’t. What I will say is, what I’m hoping for is that every one of our celebrities and partners gives the best performances of the season, and then let it fall where it falls.

The season 35 finale of DWTS airs live in every U.S. time zone, with a special three-hour finale on Tuesday at 5 p.m. PT/8 p.m. ET, simulcasting across ABC and Disney+ and streaming the next day on Hulu. Read all of THR‘s DWTS coverage here. This interview was edited and condensed for clarity.

How sci‑fi imagines sports in microgravity, and how zero‑g sports might actually work

📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1491 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Space

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sports in space have a long and proud tradition, whether it's Alan Shepard playing golf on the moon or the crew of the ISS hosting their own version of the Summer Olympics.
  • Industry observers note that not to be outdone, science fiction has expanded the idea of zero-g and low-gravity sports to their logical extent, imagining everything from Doctor Who's zero-g squash to the advanced, gamified combat simulations of Ender's Game.
  • As humanity edges closer to colonizing our neighbors through projects like the Artemis Program and its ambition to establish habitats on the moon, our imaginations have to expand to encompass not only how we'll live in space but also how we'll play.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sports in space have a long and proud tradition, whether it's Alan Shepard playing golf on the moon or the crew of the ISS hosting their own version of the Summer Olympics. The future looks bright as well, with the foundation of the Space Games Federation, the self-described "first governing and sanctioning body for competitive sports played in zero or micro-gravity," co-founded by a NASA astronaut.

Industry observers note that not to be outdone, science fiction has expanded the idea of zero-g and low-gravity sports to their logical extent, imagining everything from Doctor Who's zero-g squash to the advanced, gamified combat simulations of Ender's Game. There was even Space Jam's alien basketball game for the fate of the planet, though the gravity-defying antics there come from cartoon shenanigans rather than a zero-g playing field.

As humanity edges closer to colonizing our neighbors through projects like the Artemis Program and its ambition to establish habitats on the moon, our imaginations have to expand to encompass not only how we'll live in space but also how we'll play.

Sources indicate that we rarely think about it in an Earth context, but every sport is heavily influenced by gravity. It defines how balls arc, how promptly players can move, and even how we orient ourselves in play spaces. Remove the gravity, and all of those assumptions and mechanics evaporate as well.

Sources indicate that "First of all, in zero g, Isaac Newton will win every time," Les Johnson, former Chief Technologist for NASA, told Space. Les is a physicist with over 35 years of experience working at Marshall Space Flight Center in Huntsville, Alabama, as well as a science fiction author.

According to recent reports, "'For every action, there is an equal and opposite reaction,'" quotes Johnson. "This is very difficult to simulate in real life due to gravity; special effects often try to compensate. With today’s AI and green screens, it can actually look good on screen.".

In a recent development, in a microgravity scenario, the concept of up and down is no longer relevant. Suddenly, the playing field expands from a single, fixed plane to a fully three-dimensional space that includes height.

Sources indicate that momentum is also a completely different beast. Instead of being able to quickly stop and pivot the way you can during terrestrial sports, once you start moving in microgravity, you keep going until something stops you. It takes the trickiness of moving on ice in sports like hockey and increases it by several orders of magnitude.

Of course, the havoc wouldn't stop with maneuvering yourself. Any ball or other object would also be subject to this altered set of physics.

It has been revealed that as Johnson points out, "Aside from maneuvering the body and not tumbling or going in the wrong direction, the most difficult part would probably be throwing or hitting a ball in zero g. There would be no arc, just a straight-line throw. That would take getting used to doing, given that we’ve spent our entire lives calculating how high and fast to throw a ball in 1G so it gets to the person we intend.".

Science fiction interpretations have often leaned into these differences; in many cases, low-g sports look more like three-dimensional chess than the highly physical contests we're used to here on Earth.

Ironically, many of the best examples of space-based sports are the most grounded, where real-world physics are fully accounted for.

According to recent reports, 2013's "Ender's Game" gives us one of the best examples of a zero-g arena in space. Dubbed the "Battle Room," it's a giant hollow cube filled with obstacles. Teams enter through gates at opposite ends and participate in laser tag-style drills while having to grapple with three-dimensional space, while also finding ways to propel and protect themselves.

"The Battle Room sequence does a great job of thinking about straight‑line, constant‑velocity motion," Johnson noted. "No 'reaction' to slow you down or change your direction. Characters push off walls or each other, then drift until they hit something or fire their suit's thrusters.".

Johnson said Ender's Game also did an admirable job of showcasing how alternate physics require another layer of planning when moving through space.

"They went to great lengths to show that there was no preferred 'up' or 'down'. Again, very accurate and realistic thinking. Floating obstacles in the battle space created realistic constraints: if you don't think about where you'll rebound, you can pin yourself behind an obstacle or drift out of the fight.".

It has been revealed that recognizing how crucial play can be (and, perhaps, acknowledging ways to combat the lingering specter of space madness), real-world space agencies have begun brainstorming what recreation in low gravity might look like. Some proposed ideas include 3D ball games not wholly dissimilar from the Battle Room, where players enter a cube or spherical arena and push off walls/pass a ball in any direction, scoring by hitting targets.

Elastic tethers are another experimental concept being bandied around, where players are connected to flexible tethers to improve movement control and cut down on collisions. The Space Games Federation has also floated the idea of a version of space basketball, where the goal is guiding a magnetic ball through hoops, as well as some version of space dodgeball.

In a recent development, of course, these proposals are nothing more than thought exercises at the moment. We're a long way out from vast human populations living in zero-g environments for extended periods of time, and even further still from building spaceships capable of housing a sports hall.

NASA astronauts have experimented with trying to play various terrestrial sports in space, usually aboard the International Space Station. We've seen them playing soccer, lacrosse, and hockey with varying degrees of success.

These fun experiments mainly serve to prove what we've already suspected: that terrestrial sports can't be directly translated into a zero-g environment. We'll need upcoming rules, arenas, and whole new games if we're going to make any headway with competitive sports in space.

Sci-fi has a pretty good track record for simulating open 3D environments in microgravity. The genre also tends to do fairly well in depicting the methodical pace of moving through space and how that would affect competition (and combat).

Games like "Echo Arena" even use technology to help simulate these factors. Echo Arena is a VR game where you boost around a zero-g arena, punching opponents and trying to toss a disc into a goal.

According to recent reports, the game's innovative movement system allows players to grab almost any surface, either moving themselves along it or pushing off to float in a given direction. Players are also given wrist-mounted thrusters to let them course-correct a little, offering a respite from the unforgiving laws of motion.

Dead Space also has a section that functions similarly but with conventional game controls, though the only sport there is "don't get eaten by necromorphs.".

It has been revealed that with that mentioned, there are areas where sci-fi portrayals of zero-G games fall down. Energy levels and fatigue is a big one: constant maneuvering with your arms is exhausting, which is why real astronauts rely heavily on handholds. In a similar vein, there's the glitch of infinite momentum, specifically as it applies to rotation.

Sources indicate that johnson specifically quibbles with scenes in the Ender's Game Battle Room and "how quickly the participants can rotate their bodies or part of their bodies without going into an uncontrollable spin." He points to incidents where real-life astronauts have demonstrated how challenging this phenomenon would actually be. "I’ve watched many videos of astronauts on the ISS twist and then bounce off the wall or something. They have all looked very clumsy when they do this.".

According to recent reports, the other kind of space constraints are also often hand-waved. Even the largest existing spacecraft pale in comparison to the size of stadiums or arenas on Earth. Our early attempts at space-based sports will likely have to be centered in much smaller playing areas.

Safety issues are frequently downplayed as well; colliding with metal surfaces at high speeds in enclosed environments risks serious bodily harm to players as well as potential damage to suits/gear.

With that remarked, newer sci-fi portrayals are getting closer to reality by emphasizing slower, more deliberate movement and placing the focus on strategic thinking rather than athletic prowess.

In the meantime, astronauts might have to stick to video games to scratch their competitive itches.

Uganda minister at COP31: 'We need a just transition'

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (891 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Dw

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Ugandan Environment Minister Beatrice Atim Anywar has come to the UN climate talks in Antalya, Turkey, seeking to secure more funding for her country as it grapples with climate change.
  • "This is a thing we are living with," she told DW on the sidelines of the COP31 summit, where she's leading the Ugandan delegation.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Ugandan Environment Minister Beatrice Atim Anywar has come to the UN climate talks in Antalya, Turkey, seeking to secure more funding for her country as it grapples with climate change.

"This is a thing we are living with," she told DW on the sidelines of the COP31 summit, where she's leading the Ugandan delegation. "People are displaced, people are dying of harm, hunger. It has implications on food security and livelihoods.".

In recent years, the East African nation has been hit by a series of climate-related disasters, from deadly landslides and floods washing away villages, to droughts damaging harvests and hydroelectricity production.

"When we come to COP and we talk of what the reality is on the ground, we Ugandans have suffered it," Anywar said, referring to the effects of climate change.

"It has an implication for the health of our people, on national budgets," she added.

Recent findings suggest that climate financing for developing countries to deal with the impacts of a warming planet has become a major sticking point at this year's climate talks. The gathering of some 200 states is seeking to close gaps on how to scale up financing from developed states and whether support should be provided through grants or loans.

Africa contributes less than 4% of the global greenhouse emissions that drive rising temperatures globally, but the continent is among the most vulnerable to climate impacts.

As it deals with the effects of climate change, including extreme weather, Uganda is also rapidly expanding investment in electricity production from renewables such as hydropower and solar.

In the country of some 53 million people, more than 90% of Ugandan households still rely on wood and charcoal as the most affordable fuel for things like cooking. Biomass accounts for 90% of the country's final energy consumption.

While using wood and charcoal leads to deforestation, Ugandans have little choice. Only around 2% of the country's energy comes from electricity — which is largely derived from hydropower — and less than half of the population has access to electricity.

Industry observers note that "Now we are deliberately going into scaling up the production of electricity — hydropower electricity — and making it cheaper for cooking," Anywar noted. "We have other alternative energy sources... to mitigate this charcoal use. But the use needs to be phased out in a systematic manner by giving them alternatives.".

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video.

It has been revealed that at the same time, the country is seeking to boost economic development by becoming an oil producer. Due to open in 2027, a controversial 1,443-kilometer (897-mile) pipeline is nearly complete. It connects two oil sites in eastern Uganda with a port on the Tanzanian coast.

Environmentalists have criticized the East African Crude Oil Pipeline project, which can transport up to 246,000 barrels per day. Environmentalists say it runs counter to the goal of limiting global temperature rise and could damage fragile ecosystems.

The Climate Accountability Institute mentioned it would release 379 million tons of climate-heating pollution over its 20-year lifetime.

Oil wells for the project, operated by French energy giant TotalEnergies, are also located in Uganda's largest and oldest national park, Murchison Falls.

"That has been also a sticky issue. And actually, that is one of the challenges we are facing at COPs," Anywar said. She stressed that measures have been taken to limit emissions, and that the project was progressing in a "very deliberate way.".

The minister also urged developed countries to cut less wealthy nations some slack for using the resources they have to drive much-needed development, saying oil revenues could help fund the transition to cleaner energy.

"You cannot tell us to cut off the umbilical cord that feeds us, as much as it has to be cut off," Anywar noted, criticizing the lack of financing from developed countries to deal with climate change. "We are here begging for funds that are not forthcoming.".

Anywar added that developing countries "need a just transition," referring to an equitable shift away from fossil fuels that focuses on protecting workers and communities.

Another way Uganda is looking to finance climate change adaptation is through carbon credits, Anywar noted, describing them as a potential "breakthrough.".

Carbon credits are tradeable permits representing one ton of carbon dioxide that has been reduced or removed from the atmosphere through initiatives such as forest protection, renewable energy projects or tree planting schemes. Companies or governments can buy them to offset emissions they have not cut themselves.

"Our country is rich with biodiversity. And that is what we are looking forward to — attracting investors into our natural setup so that we earn some finances," Anywar mentioned.

Carbon credits have been promoted as an key source of income for developing countries. But they have also faced criticism, for a lack of transparency and allowing polluting activities to continue.

Recent findings suggest that "We need to have a bankable approach to all interventions. Otherwise… it's not going to work for us," Anywar said, adding that her country also wants to attract investment and build partnerships in smart agriculture and the energy transition.

"If we rely on begging for funds which are not forthcoming, we shall go back empty handed.".

Scientists say the human family tree may need a radical rewrite

📅 21 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1146 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sciencedaily

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that the human family tree may be due for a major rewrite.
  • The study, published in the American Journal of Biological Anthropology, proposes a sweeping change to how we organize millions of years of human evolution.
  • That would mean bringing groups such as Australopithecus and Paranthropus, which have traditionally been classified separately, into the same genus as modern humans.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that the human family tree may be due for a major rewrite. New research from Monash University challenges the traditional way scientists classify our ancient ancestors, suggesting that several groups long considered separate from humans may actually belong within our own genus, Homo.

The study, published in the American Journal of Biological Anthropology, proposes a sweeping change to how we organize millions of years of human evolution. Its central argument is that all human species and their closely related fossil relatives from the past 4 to 5 million years should be classified within the genus Homo.

That would mean bringing groups such as Australopithecus and Paranthropus, which have traditionally been classified separately, into the same genus as modern humans. Although these ancient relatives differed considerably in appearance, anatomy, and behavior, the researchers argue that the evolutionary boundaries separating them are becoming increasingly difficult to justify.

Why the Human Family Tree May Need to Be Redrawn.

Human evolution is frequently illustrated as a relatively orderly progression, beginning with ancestors that resembled apes and gradually moving through species such as Australopithecus and early Homo before arriving at modern humans, Homo sapiens.

Industry observers note that however, evolution did not unfold as a simple sequence in which one species neatly replaced another. Instead, the fossil evidence reveals a complicated family tree with numerous branches, overlapping species, and evolutionary relationships that scientists are still working to understand.

Each fresh fossil discovery can complicate that picture. Traits once believed to distinguish one group of ancient human relatives from another have increasingly been found across multiple groups, making it harder to determine where traditional classifications should begin and end.

It has been revealed that dr. Ian Towle, a Research Fellow at the Monash Biomedicine Discovery Institute and lead researcher on the study, argues that these discoveries are exposing weaknesses in the existing classification system. This applies not only to species already assigned to Homo, but also to members of Australopithecus and Paranthropus, groups that lived during the past 5 million years.

"Recent fossil discoveries and advances in evolutionary and genetic analysis make this an ideal time to reconsider whether our traditional taxonomy still accurately reflects human evolution," Dr. Towle noted.

"These groups do not necessarily represent distinct evolutionary branches, or 'clades', and differences in behavior and ecology once used to distinguish them have also become increasingly difficult to maintain.

"I propose expanding Homo to include these other groups to provide a more accurate and stable way to represent the complex evolutionary relationships revealed by the growing fossil record.".

How Scientists Classify Our Ancient Ancestors.

To understand the proposed change, it helps to look at how scientists organize living and extinct organisms.

The system is known as taxonomy, which involves naming species and arranging them into groups based on their characteristics and evolutionary relationships.

Recent findings suggest that A genus is one level of this system, sitting above the species level. Modern humans, for example, belong to the species Homo sapiens, with Homo identifying our genus and sapiens identifying our species.

According to recent reports, over the past 50 years, advances in evolutionary research have significantly changed how scientists approach classification. Rather than relying primarily on physical similarities, modern taxonomy increasingly seeks to organize species according to their actual evolutionary ancestry.

Sources indicate that an notable concept in this approach is the clade. A clade consists of a common ancestor and all of its descendants. By grouping organisms this way, scientists aim to produce classifications that accurately reflect the branches of the evolutionary tree.

In a recent development, this approach has become increasingly influential in biology over recent decades. However, Towle argues that the classification of our own evolutionary relatives has been slower to adopt these principles consistently.

Why Brain Size and Tool Use No Longer Define Humans.

Traditionally, scientists have distinguished members of the genus Homo from other ancient human relatives using a combination of physical and behavioral characteristics.

These have included relatively large brains, sophisticated tool use, and particular anatomical features associated with human evolution.

But discoveries over recent decades have challenged the reliability of those distinctions.

Scientists have identified members of Homo with surprisingly small brains, demonstrating that a large brain was not necessarily a defining characteristic of every species in our genus.

At the same time, evidence suggests that species traditionally placed in Australopithecus and Paranthropus likely displayed more complex behaviors than researchers once assumed.

Sources indicate that together, these findings have weakened the boundaries used to separate the three groups. Characteristics once thought to be exclusive to Homo may have been shared more widely among our ancient relatives.

As a result, determining which species belong within the human genus has become increasingly complicated. Towle argues that the problem may lie not with the fossil evidence, but with the classification system scientists are trying to fit it into.

A Radical Proposal for 5 Million Years of Human Evolution.

Towle's proposed solution is to expand the genus Homo to include species right now classified as Australopithecus and Paranthropus.

The idea is not that these ancient relatives were identical to modern humans or possessed all the traits associated with our species. Rather, the broader classification would recognize their evolutionary connections while still allowing scientists to distinguish among individual species.

According to recent reports, such a change could also make human taxonomy more stable. Instead of repeatedly revising the boundaries between major groups whenever newly introduced fossils are uncovered, scientists could use a broader genus that accommodates the diversity revealed by ongoing discoveries.

The proposal represents a significant departure from traditional classifications, and it remains a scientific argument rather than an officially adopted change. Nevertheless, it highlights how much our understanding of human origins has evolved as new evidence has accumulated.

"The more we learn about our ancestors and close fossil relatives, the more we realize how complex and non-linear our family tree is," Dr. Towle remarked.

"Expanding the Homo genus to also include species of Australopithecus and Paranthropus will allow us to account for differences without regularly reclassifying particular groups.".

It has been revealed that ultimately, the research raises a fundamental question about how scientists define the human family. If the traits once used to separate our ancestors are not as distinctive as previously believed, the names and categories used to describe millions of years of human evolution may need to change along with our understanding of the past.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

IATSE Local One, which represents stagehands on Broadway, has reached a tentative agreement with the Broadway League, ahead of the lucrative holiday weeks.

It has been revealed that this comes after Local One members had voted to authorize a strike in October, after working on an expired contract since late July. If called, a work stoppage from Local One would have likely put a halt to most Broadway indicates. The agreement still needs to be ratified by members of the union, with details of the tentative agreement planned to be available ahead of the union’s December meeting.

However, another local chapter of the union, IATSE Local 764, which represents Broadway dressers and others who work on costumes, still remains without a contract, and voted Sunday to authorize a strike if necessary.

Local 764 members have been bargaining with The Broadway League, a trade association for Broadway producers and general managers, since June. The members’ previous agreement had expired July 26. The League cancelled bargaining sessions scheduled for November 18 and 19, according to IATSE, and Local 764 has been pushing for new dates.

Industry observers note that IATSE stated the issues still in contention include wages and a gender pay gap that has existed for decades for Broadway wardrobe workers. The field is predominantly female, and has been paid “significantly lower rates than stagehand classifications historically held predominantly by men” according to the union, with Local 764 department heads needing to work 45 percent longer to earn pay comparable to workers in similar department-head roles.

Both Actors’ Equity and the American Federation of Musicians Local 802 also voted to authorize strikes last year, and came very close to doing so, before striking new contracts with the Broadway League.

#185052. Scientists turn Moon dust into LEGO-like bricks for future lunar bases

General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Sciencedaily ↗ Open Full Page

Scientists turn Moon dust into LEGO-like bricks for future lunar bases

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (975 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sciencedaily

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, building permanent bases on the Moon could become much easier if astronauts can turn the material beneath their feet into construction supplies.
  • The study, published in NPJ Advanced Manufacturing, was led by first author Cole McCallum, who was an undergraduate student at the University of Arkansas when the research was conducted.
  • To manufacture the bricks, the team used a 3D printing technique known as laser powder bed fusion.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, building permanent bases on the Moon could become much easier if astronauts can turn the material beneath their feet into construction supplies. Researchers at the University of Arkansas have demonstrated a method for 3D printing simulated lunar dust into interlocking, LEGO-like bricks. The approach could eventually allow NASA to produce building materials directly on the Moon, reducing the amount of equipment and supplies that must be transported from Earth.

The study, published in NPJ Advanced Manufacturing, was led by first author Cole McCallum, who was an undergraduate student at the University of Arkansas when the research was conducted. Wan Shou, an assistant professor of mechanical engineering at the university, served as senior author.

To manufacture the bricks, the team used a 3D printing technique known as laser powder bed fusion. The process begins by spreading a thin layer of powder across a flat surface. A concentrated light source heats the particles until they fuse together, a process called sintering. The printing platform then moves downward, allowing another layer of powder to be added and fused. Repeating these steps gradually produces a solid three-dimensional object.

Unlike Earth's soil, lunar regolith contains no organic material. Instead, it is made up of sharp, irregular fragments produced by billions of years of impacts from asteroids, micrometeorites, and other debris striking the Moon. Because actual lunar material is difficult to obtain, the researchers worked with a commercially available substitute called Lunar Highlands Regolith Simulant (LHS-1). This material is designed to resemble samples brought back by NASA's Apollo missions during the 1960s and early 1970s.

Turning Moon Dust Into Bricks Without Added Binders.

Previous efforts to 3D print structures from lunar regolith have relied on additional substances called binders to hold the particles together. Although these materials can improve the strength of printed objects, they introduce a major logistical challenge: the binders would need to be delivered from Earth.

The University of Arkansas team demonstrated a different approach. Using a relatively low-power light source, they became the first researchers to directly fuse simulated lunar regolith into interlocking, reconfigurable construction blocks without adding a binding agent. Instead of relying on another material to hold the structure together, the lunar dust particles bond directly with one another.

Recent findings suggest that "There's nothing else it's binding to. The regolith powder is binding to itself," McCallum stated.

The team produced small bricks measuring a few centimeters across, including pieces shaped like crosses and the letter H. Their interlocking designs allow the blocks to fit together in a manner similar to LEGO pieces, potentially making it possible to assemble larger structures from individual printed components.

However, the experimental bricks are not yet ready for demanding construction applications. Compared with objects manufactured using binders, the blocks made entirely from simulated lunar regolith contain more internal pores and have lower structural strength.

Recent findings suggest that "These structures we're making can be self-supported," McCallum said. "But I would be hesitant to say our process could be used for something that's supporting other loads at this moment yet.".

Challenges Ahead for Building Lunar Bases.

It has been revealed that before this technology can be considered for actual construction on the Moon, several notable questions must be answered. Shou explained that scientists still need to determine how the printing process would behave under the Moon's low-gravity conditions and in a vacuum. The strength and durability of the finished bricks must also be improved to make them suitable for practical applications.

Recent findings suggest that despite these challenges, Shou believes the technique could eventually offer an efficient way to manufacture construction components and larger structures for permanent lunar settlements. The ability to produce interlocking bricks from locally available material could be especially valuable as NASA works toward establishing a sustained human presence on the Moon.

How Undergraduate Research Helped Drive the Discovery.

For McCallum, the lunar construction project was also an opportunity to gain valuable scientific experience early in his education. Originally from Little Rock, Arkansas, he joined Shou's laboratory during the early stages of his undergraduate studies at the University of Arkansas.

"He had this really strong belief that undergrads should get involved more with research," McCallum stated.

In a recent development, mcCallum graduated in May with two degrees, one in mechanical engineering and another in physics. His academic achievements also earned him a place in the inaugural class of Lafayette Fellows, a competitive program that selected just 30 students from a pool of more than 3,400 applicants. Established to commemorate the 250th anniversary of the United States, the fellowship supports students pursuing master's degrees in France.

He is now studying aerospace engineering in Toulouse at the Institut Supérieur de l'Aéronautique et de l'Espace, also known as ISAE-SUPAERO, which ranks among France's leading aerospace engineering institutions.

Although his current studies have taken him in a different direction from the additive manufacturing research he conducted in Shou's laboratory, McCallum credits the experience with helping him develop essential research skills. Working through experimental difficulties and learning from unsuccessful attempts gave him a valuable foundation for future scientific work.

According to recent reports, "It helps you refine and overcome all the problems you have as a researcher. There are a lot of mistakes that I made the first time through," he stated. "It was really nice to have a head start on everyone else and make those mistakes early.".

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

HSBC’s top brass defended their strategy Monday to frustrated shareholders in the lender’s largest market, as Europe’s biggest bank continued to face calls to be split up.

At an informal shareholder meeting in Hong Kong, Chairman Mark Tucker and CEO Noel Quinn took questions from investors on complications ranging from how the bank was approaching demands for an overhaul of its business to its purchase of Silicon Valley Bank’s UK arm.

In prepared remarks, Tucker and Quinn each reiterated the board’s recommendation that shareholders vote against a resolution on the docket for its annual general meeting in May that would force the bank to come up with a strategy to spin off or reorganize its Asian business — the lender’s main source of profits.

HSBC's biggest shareholder reignites debate about breaking up the bank.

Tucker remarked the board was unanimous in its opposition to the resolution, stating plainly: “It would not be in your interest to split the bank.”.

He said the board had previously reviewed a range of options for restructuring the bank, and concluded that such alternatives would “materially destroy value for shareholders,” including dividends.

“Our strategy is working,” Tucker told the room of more than 1,000 shareholders. “Our current strategy is moving dividends up.”.

HSBC has been facing calls to separate its Asian business from the rest of the bank over the past year.

Shareholders in Hong Kong — where HSBC is a mainstay of many retail investors’ portfolios — contend that the London-based lender’s performance has been dragged down by its businesses in other regions.

Quinn addressed those complaints head-on Monday, saying “our profits in Hong Kong and the UK are no longer being dragged down by underperformance elsewhere. The group is performing well as a whole.”.

Pressed later by a shareholder on the issue, Quinn said a breakup of the bank would result in “significant revenue loss” because much of its business relied on cross-border transactions.

Investors have also been unhappy with HSBC scrapping its dividend in 2020, at the request of British regulators. They argue that if the lender cordoned off its activities in Asia, it would no longer have to expose Hong Kong shareholders to requests in other jurisdictions.

Christine Fong, a district council member in Hong Kong, stated she represented about 500 small shareholders who had been affected by the dividend cancellation.

“Street hawkers, taxi drivers or teachers — they all relied on the dividend to pay for their regular expenses, like mortgage, insurance payments, school fees,” Fong told CNN.

“That’s why, three years ago, what HSBC did upset those small minority shareholders.”.

Fong has now joined calls for shareholders to vote in favor of the proposal for the bank to spin off its Asian business, despite the lender bringing back its dividend in 2021, albeit at a lower level.

Ken Lui, an activist shareholder in Hong Kong who put the resolution together, doubled down on his call for support ahead of the meeting Monday.

The resolution will require 75% of votes to be passed in May, but “nothing is impossible,” he told reporters outside the meeting venue.

Lui, who said he personally held a stake worth 100 million Hong Kong dollars ($12.7 million), laid out aims for his team to focus on “targeted outreach to institutional shareholders to present our case and gain their support.”.

His group will also canvass 18 districts of Hong Kong “to tell HSBC shareholders that they finally have a chance to speak for themselves and protect their rights through voting,” he added.

HSBC is also facing pressure from its largest shareholder.

Ping An (PNGAY), China’s biggest insurer, holds an 8% stake in HSBC and has backed calls for the bank to rethink its structure.

In a series of remarks made public by the Chinese firm last November, Huang Yong, chairman of Ping An’s asset management arm, said “we will support any initiatives including a spinoff that are conducive to improve HSBC’s performance and value.”.

Since then, the insurance giant’s views haven’t changed, according to a person familiar with the matter.

The source told CNN that Ping An has been calling for HSBC to explore a reorganization, with an eye on boosting its valuation and simplifying its regulatory obligations around the globe.

The insurer has not recommended a specific path forward but will support any initiatives, including a spinoff of its Asian business, that could boost its stock performance or value, the person added. Ping An did not immediately respond to a request for comment on how it planned to vote at the upcoming general meeting.

Sources indicate that HSBC’s leaders were also asked Monfday why the bank had scooped up the British unit of SVB following the stunning collapse of its parent in the United States. The purchase was made for £1 ($1.20) last month, just days after SVB had folded.

Critics have questioned HSBC’s ability to perform adequate due diligence on SVB UK’s customers because of how rapidly the deal came together.

“Did HSBC look into the clients of SVB in detail? Say, the financial statement — whether they can pay back the loan?” stated Fong.

HSBC buys SVB's UK business, ending 'nightmare' for British tech.

Quinn and Tucker defended the acquisition, calling it a good business opportunity that allowed the bank to gain hundreds of innovative startups as customers. They pushed back on the notion that management hadn’t had time to carry out proper due diligence.

Tucker also weighed in on recent tumult in the banking industry, saying he did not expect an “immediate impact” on HSBC.

“After the collapse of a number of smaller regional banks and the takeover of Credit Suisse, the share prices of all banks have been suppressed,” he noted.

In a recent development, but he noted he did not believe such developments represented “a systemic risk” to the sector. “I do expect a period of uncertainty” before nerves settle, he added.

Latest Update: CERN scientists finally find evidence of a particle decay so rare it took 40 years to detect

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1451 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sciencedaily

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that after more than four decades of searching, physicists at CERN have finally found evidence of an extraordinarily rare particle decay that occurs only about once in every 10 billion beauty particles.
  • The evidence comes from the upgraded LHCb experiment at CERN's Large Hadron Collider (LHC).
  • Sources indicate that the elusive process, called 'Bd to mu mu', has a statistical significance of 3.2 sigma.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that after more than four decades of searching, physicists at CERN have finally found evidence of an extraordinarily rare particle decay that occurs only about once in every 10 billion beauty particles. The long-awaited result could help scientists investigate a largely unexplored realm of physics where unknown particles and forces of nature may exist.

The evidence comes from the upgraded LHCb experiment at CERN's Large Hadron Collider (LHC). Researchers at the University of Manchester played important roles in the international effort, contributing to the advanced technology that made the measurement possible.

Sources indicate that the elusive process, called 'Bd to mu mu', has a statistical significance of 3.2 sigma. That is strong enough to qualify as evidence, but physicists will need additional data before they can officially declare a discovery. Even so, the finding marks a major milestone in a search that has lasted more than 40 years.

It also creates newly introduced opportunities to test the Standard Model, the leading scientific framework describing fundamental particles and how they interact. By examining this exceptionally rare decay in greater detail, researchers hope to uncover subtle clues that could eventually point toward physics beyond our current understanding.

Why Rare Particle Decays Could Reveal New Physics.

The LHCb experiment specializes in studying particles that contain beauty quarks. These are heavier relatives of the up and down quarks that make up much of the ordinary matter around us.

When particles collide inside the Large Hadron Collider, enormous numbers of beauty quarks are produced. However, they survive for only about one and a half trillionths of a second before decaying into other particles.

Scientists study these transformations because they may reveal the influence of particles that cannot be directly observed at the collider. By measuring exactly how frequently different decays occur, physicists can search for unexpected effects that might indicate previously unknown physics.

Particularly rare decays offer an vital advantage. Because they happen so infrequently, their rates can be especially sensitive to contributions from undiscovered particles. Even small differences between predicted and observed decay rates could provide valuable evidence of fresh forces or particles.

A One in 10 Billion Particle Decay.

The newly observed signal involves a process known as 'Bd to mu mu'. During this decay, a particle containing a beauty quark transforms into two muons, which are heavier relatives of electrons.

Sources indicate that according to theoretical predictions, this transformation should occur only about once in every 10 billion beauty particles. Despite decades of investigation, no individual experiment had previously produced convincing evidence that it occurs.

According to recent reports, the upgraded LHCb experiment has now achieved a statistical significance of 3.2 sigma. Although this meets the standard for reporting evidence, particle physicists generally require a significance of five sigma before announcing a confirmed discovery.

Professor Chris Parkes, Head of the Department of Physics and Astronomy at the University of Manchester, led the international LHCb collaboration during construction of its major upgrade. He also oversaw the collaboration's approval of the newly introduced findings.

He explained: "The upgraded LHCb was a major undertaking -- a fifteen-year design and construction project from a 1900 international member collaboration.

"The UK made the largest national contribution to the project, pioneering newly introduced technologies that have made today's result possible, where we probe nature at a new scale. But this is also just the start; we are planning the construction of an experiment that will exploit the capabilities of the next-generation High Luminosity LHC, probing physics at an even smaller scale.".

Parkes, who became a Fellow of the Royal Society earlier this year in recognition of his contributions to LHCb, offered a memorable comparison to illustrate just how improbable the decay is.

"This decay is remarkably unlikely; the chance of it happening is roughly like going on a romantic date and, on your very first try, finding the one perfect match for you among everyone on Earth.".

Advanced LHC Detectors Make the Breakthrough Possible.

Detecting such an uncommon event requires instruments capable of following the movements of particles with extraordinary accuracy.

One of the most important components of the upgraded LHCb experiment is a silicon pixel detector developed with major contributions from researchers in the United Kingdom. Called the Vertex Locator, it measures the paths of particles generated during collisions inside the collider.

Positioned just five millimeters from the LHC beams, the detector allows researchers to determine precisely where particles originate and where they subsequently decay.

Dr. Stefano De Capua, who directed detector construction at the University of Manchester, described the extensive collaboration behind the technology.

Recent findings suggest that "We worked with nearly 90 UK companies to construct this detector and trained the next generation of scientists and engineers on the novel technologies we are using. It is these detectors that we use to locate where the beauty meson was produced and pinpoint where it decayed into two muons.".

The wider LHCb upgrade also allows the experiment to gather information at up to five times its previous rate. This greater capacity, together with improvements in tracking technology, is helping physicists identify events that were previously too difficult to measure reliably.

Exploring the Mysterious Zeptoverse.

Beyond confirming an exceptionally rare particle process, the result could help scientists investigate what they call the 'Zeptoverse'.

This name refers to an almost unimaginably small scale, measured in zeptometers. A single zeptometer is just a billionth of a trillionth of a meter. Physicists suspect that effects from presently unknown particles and forces could become apparent when nature is examined at these extreme scales.

For now, the fresh measurement agrees with the Standard Model. Researchers have not found evidence that the established theory is wrong, but increasingly precise measurements could reveal deviations that current experiments cannot yet detect.

Such differences would be especially significant because they could indicate where the Standard Model stops providing a complete explanation of the physical world.

Professor Conor Fitzpatrick of the University of Manchester, who serves as Deputy Physics Coordinator of the international LHCb collaboration, emphasized the importance of finally obtaining the long-sought signal.

Sources indicate that "There has been a more than forty year long search by physicists worldwide to observe this decay. It is a golden channel to observe the effects of newly introduced physics from beyond our current knowledge.

It has been revealed that "The results from this experiment are expanding our understanding of nature at its most fundamental level. We are excited to have finally seen this elusive signal and looking forward to the future discoveries that will come from our data.".

What Comes Next for CERN's Particle Research?

The upgraded LHCb experiment is expected to continue gathering a substantially larger collection of measurements into the early 2030s. With more data, physicists should be able to determine the frequency of this rare decay with much greater precision.

It has been revealed that researchers are also planning another major upgrade that could increase data collection rates by an additional factor of ten. This would improve their ability to investigate extremely rare particle processes and search for the effects of unknown particles at even smaller distance scales.

Professor Brian Cox, a particle physicist at the University of Manchester who did not participate in the experiment, highlighted how improvements in scientific instruments can lead to crucial advances in understanding nature.

"This is an key result and a beautiful example of how science advances. We upgrade our instruments, and we see nature in greater detail. Occasionally we see something we don't understand, and then progress is made. We cannot know whether this progress will be incremental or genuinely world-changing -- that's science! LHCb is a major scientific success.".

According to recent reports, the experiment receives funding from the Science and Technology Facilities Council, which operates within UK Research and Innovation. The UK LHCb collaboration brings together scientists from ten universities across the United Kingdom and the STFC Rutherford Appleton Laboratory.

Although the newly detected decay has not yet revealed any unknown particles or forces, it gives physicists a powerful newly introduced way to search for them. After more than 40 years of effort, an extraordinarily elusive process is finally becoming accessible to detailed study, potentially bringing researchers closer to understanding some of the universe's deepest mysteries.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Being a member of Capitol society in Panem is an honor not to be taken lightly, at least if you’re Drusilla Sickle, played by screen legend Glenn Close in “The Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping.”.

Recent findings suggest that in the book, Drusilla is the cruel and vain escort for Haymitch Abernathy (Joseph Zada) and the rest of the District 12 tributes in the 50th Hunger Games, where she uses over-the-top fashion to broadcast her social status. Close worked closely with costume designer Bina Daigeler and hair, makeup and prosthetics designer Natalie MacGowan Spencer to ensure the character translated properly from Suzanne Collins’ bestselling prequel novel to the screen. Related Stories Jane Lynch Wants to Return for 'Glee' Reboot: 'I Would Love to Do Sue Sylvester for the Rest of My Life' Chris Colfer Notes 'Glee' Reboot 'Conversations' About Kurt's Return Are Ongoing: 'From What I Heard, It Sounded Very Funny and Like a Good Idea'.

One challenge Daigeler faced was meeting Close’s request that each outfit felt connected, creating a through line that explained why Drusilla changes from one look to the next. Despite the drastic differences between each outfit, Daigeler established continuity through the character’s accessories, most notably a collection of gold medals and military-inspired epaulets that created a sense of authority.

“She wears all these medals, because somehow she thinks she is the top general of the capital,” Daigeler tells Variety.

And, not dissimilar to red-bottomed Louboutin shoes, Daigeler gave Drusilla dramatically long black nails that were painted red underneath to show her abundant wealth.

It has been revealed that the character’s Capitol allegiance also went beyond her wardrobe, with Spencer overseeing her hair and makeup. While creating the looks, Spencer relied heavily on Collins’ source material to remain faithful to the author’s vision. Collins describes Drusilla as having implanted tabs that pull the skin on her face back, which Spencer wanted to honor. But because there wasn’t enough time each morning for an extensive prosthetics process, Spencer turned to Hollywood tape to tightly pull Close’s skin back, creating a distorted appearance. She later added tabs on the sides of Close’s face to complete the illusion, along with fake teeth that heightened Drusilla’s “scary” and “eerie” appearance.

“[Glenn] really wanted to pull it so taut that it changed all of her facial features, which it really did,” Spencer tells Variety.

According to recent reports, daigeler and Spencer’s shared mission: to create visuals that resonate with the franchise’s devoted fans — who “know their stuff inside out,” Spencer quips. “They’re so passionate.” When the book was released and casting announcements began rolling out, Spencer would regularly check social media to see what fans envisioned for the adaptation and what details they hoped to see on screen.

Below, Spencer and Daigeler break down the process of creating each of Drusilla’s costumes, hair and makeup, as well as the inspiration behind each look.

It has been revealed that drusilla makes her grand entrance at the District 12 reaping, wheeled into the frame wearing a bold yellow ensemble. The outfit is a stark contrast to the muted colors worn throughout Panem’s poorest district — the exact irony Spencer and Daigeler hoped to portray by making that the character’s brightest look in the film.

“It shouldn’t have any practicality. That is why she was driven in,” Daigeler states of the tightly-cinched yellow coat dress. “It was supposed to be very stiff.”.

Recent findings suggest that to complement the dress’ high collar, Spencer styled Close with an orange bob that also paid homage to the film’s ‘70s aesthetic. At Close’s request, the look was completed with a raven headpiece — which, to be clear, was not an intentional nod to Lenore Dove’s name poem.

Industry observers note that “For me, that sort of represents the children of the district — something that’s taxidermied and dead on their head,” Spencer claims about the headpiece. “And [Drusilla’s] so proud of that statement.”.

It has been revealed that black medals and military-inspired shoulder plates further accentuated the ensemble, reinforcing Drusilla’s self-appointed authority. “She looked like a yellow general,” Daigeler adds.

When representing District 12 at the Capitol’s chariot parade, Drusilla’s color palette dims to an all-black look that publicly links her to the district’s coal-mining industry. To elevate the outfit and solidify her Capitol status, Daigeler experimented with different textures to create the illusion of leatherlike skin while also keeping her gold medals and fringed military epaulets.

Recent findings suggest that “We wanted to give it strength,” Daigeler notes of the outfit, which, she notes, also signals that things are getting more serious in the film’s storyline. “We wanted it to be a little bit aggressive and very demanding. And very Capitol.”.

It has been revealed that close initially wanted to style the look with an extravagant, fluffy hat, but she and Spencer ultimately settled on a simpler black wig with pointed horns so as not to distract from Drusilla’s face. The shorter bangs draw more attention to the exaggerated eye makeup and the face-slimming tabs.

Drusilla settles on a softer green dress for the tributes’ interviews with Caesar Flickerman (Kieran Culkin), which once again challenged Daigeler to maintain the character’s threads between outfit changes.

It has been revealed that “Where’s the strength? Where’s the craziness?” she asked herself when accessorizing Drusilla’s third look, a crepey, olive-hued gown with a high neck and massive, billowy sleeves.

This time, Daigeler forwent Drusilla’s medallions and instead made a statement by adding red gloves, tights and boots, paired with spiky necklaces.

Sources indicate that spencer leaned further into the softer ensemble by adding a wave to Drusilla’s hair, washed with a light shade of pink. “I really like fabrics and the colors and how the hair and makeup is going to be one big look altogether,” Spencer notes.

It has been revealed that drusilla’s final appearance comes after Haymitch is declared the victor of the 50th Hunger Games — or, at least in Drusilla’s mind, after she is declared the victor. Complete with a purple sash, the look was designed to make it seem as if Drusilla herself had won the games.

This was the only outfit not described in Collins’ novel, giving Daigeler the creative freedom to execute her own vision. Knowing Drusilla would appear on the colorful stage, she wanted to put her in a bold red ensemble that would ensure she stood out.

Without a predetermined silhouette in mind, Daigeler drew inspiration from designers Alexander McQueen, Talyano and Balenciaga, as well as Renaissance-era shapes.

Sources indicate that “I went to a beautiful fabric store in London, and I just found all these beautiful, different textured red fabrics,” Daigeler indicates. “I didn’t have it clear what would be the silhouette of the dress, but I knew that it should be an evening gown and somehow huge and over the top.”.

Spencer completed the transformation by leaning into the showgirl-inspired makeup, settling on a bright red lip and feathered hair.

It has been revealed that “[Drusilla’s] like a performer. When you really do think about it, she’s a narcissist. ‘This is me. I’m bold. I’m dominant,’” Spencer notes. “We had all the showgirls — all of those massive colors and the feathers and everything else, so it’s almost like a carnival of entertainers coming together on the stage. The set design, the colors, all the background people in the crowd are so, so notable. What you’re portraying is a performance. It’s entertainment, and that’s who they are.”.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

MARSHALL, Mich. — Ford Motor has started producing battery cells in the U.S. for its next generation of electric vehicles using technologies licensed by Chinese battery giant CATL.

Recent findings suggest that the automaker remarked Wednesday that cell production at a $3 billion plant in Marshall, Michigan — roughly 100 miles west of Detroit — started last month and the cells are now shipping out. They'll be used in prototypes for its Fathom small electric pickup truck, which CEO Jim Farley has touted as rivaling Tesla and Chinese competitors.

According to recent reports, the production marks a milestone for the Detroit automaker and is the next step toward using lower-cost lithium iron phosphate, or LFP, battery cells in U.S. vehicles. The technology was created in the U.S. but commercialized largely in China.

The automaker's decision to make the batteries at the roughly 2 million-square-foot facility has been criticized by some lawmakers and U.S. Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy over Ford's ties to CATL.

According to recent reports, alan Clarke, Ford's vice president of advanced development projects, said licensing the technology from CATL helped the automaker bring the low-cost battery chemistry to the U.S. as quickly as possible.

"If we want to get to being able to produce affordable EVs in the United States, we need to also do it the fastest way possible," Clarke noted Tuesday during a tour of the facility. "CATL being the biggest in the world means that they're the best supplier to get us that technology and help us learn ourselves how to produce LFP cells.".

The U.S. government has increased scrutiny of Chinese ties with U.S. companies even as President Donald Trump is meeting this week with Chinese leader Xi Jinping and Russian President Vladimir Putin.

In September, Duffy sent a letter to Farley expressing "profound concern" about Ford's ties to Chinese companies that it believes could be detrimental to the Detroit carmaker and the U.S. automotive industry. The White House a day later followed up by commending the automaker for its domestic jobs and manufacturing.

Sources indicate that ford — the largest producer of U.S. vehicles — has routinely touted its American roots, jobs and manufacturing, especially as the Biden and Trump administrations have pushed to onshore and grow U.S. production.

According to recent reports, ford's battery plant in Marshall is expected to be capable of producing 40 battery cells a minute, equating to 20 gigawatt-hours annually for EVs and the manufacturer's energy storage business. That's down from initial intends of up to 40 gigawatt-hours annually amid an EV pullback by the automaker and broader industry.

Ford has said the production pace will help reduce battery costs and that the facility has room for additional capacity if needed.

The facility is highly automated, but Ford noted it's still in the early stages of certifying its processes, as it plans to ramp up cell production next year before the expected launch of the Fathom pickup during the fourth quarter of 2027.

#185039. Breaking: A 50-year-old theory about evolution may have been wrong all along

📅 21 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 6m • 📚 Deep Dive (1258 w)
