A upcoming approach to a Covid-19 nasal vaccine reveals early promise

📅 03 Apr 2023 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1468 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: CNN

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Scientists in Germany say they’ve been able to make a nasal vaccine that can shut down a Covid-19 infection in the nose and throat, where the virus gets its first foothold in the body.
  • In experiments in hamsters, two doses of the vaccine – which is made with a live but weakened form of the coronavirus that causes Covid-19 – blocked the virus from copying itself in the animals’ upper airways, achieving “sterilizing immunity” and preventing illness, a long-sought goal of the pandemic.
  • WHO experts revise Covid-19 vaccine advice, say healthy kids and teens low risk.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Scientists in Germany say they’ve been able to make a nasal vaccine that can shut down a Covid-19 infection in the nose and throat, where the virus gets its first foothold in the body.

In experiments in hamsters, two doses of the vaccine – which is made with a live but weakened form of the coronavirus that causes Covid-19 – blocked the virus from copying itself in the animals’ upper airways, achieving “sterilizing immunity” and preventing illness, a long-sought goal of the pandemic.

WHO experts revise Covid-19 vaccine advice, say healthy kids and teens low risk.

Although this vaccine has several more hurdles to clear before it gets to a doctor’s office or drug store, other nasal vaccines are in use or are nearing the finish line in clinical trials.

Sources indicate that china and India both rolled out vaccines given through the nasal tissues last fall, though it’s not clear how well they may be working. Studies on the effectiveness of these vaccines have yet to be published, leaving much of the world to wonder whether this approach to protection really works in people.

The US has reached something of a stalemate with Covid-19. Even with the darkest days of the pandemic behind us, hundreds of Americans are still dying daily as the infection continues to simmer in the background of our return to normal life.

In a recent development, as long as the virus continues to spread among people and animals, there’s always the potential for it mutate into a more contagious or more damaging version of itself. And while Covid infections have become manageable for most healthy people, they may still pose a danger to vulnerable groups such as the elderly and immunocompromised.

Researchers hope next-generation Covid-19 vaccines, which aim to shut down the virus before it ever gets a chance to make us sick and ultimately prevent the spread of infection, could make our newest resident respiratory infection less of a threat.

China approves its first mRNA Covid-19 vaccine.

One way scientists are trying to do that is by boosting mucosal immunity, beefing up immune defenses in the tissues that line the upper airways, right where the virus would land and begin to infect our cells.

It’s a bit like stationing firefighters underneath the smoke alarm in your house, claims study author Emanuel Wyler, a scientist at the Max Delbruck Center for Molecular Medicine in the Helmholtz Association in Berlin.

The immunity that’s created by shots works throughout the body, but it resides primarily in the blood. That means it may take longer to mount a response.

“If they are already on site, they can immediately eliminate the fire, but if they’re like 2 miles away, they first need to drive there, and by that time, one-third of the house is already in full flames,” Wyler remarked.

Mucosal vaccines are also better at priming a different kind of first responder than injections do. They do a better job of summoning IgA antibodies, which have four arms to grab onto invaders instead of the two arms that the y-shaped IgG antibodies have. Some scientists think IgA antibodies may be less picky about their targets than IgG antibodies, which makes them better equipped to deal with fresh variants.

It has been revealed that the upcoming nasal vaccine takes a new approach to a very old idea: weakening a virus so it’s no longer a threat and then giving it to people so their immune systems can learn to recognize and fight it off. The first vaccines using this approach date to the 1870s, against anthrax and rabies. Back then, scientists weakened the agents they were using with heat and chemicals.

Recent findings suggest that the researchers manipulated the genetic material in the virus to make it harder for cells to translate. This technique, called codon pair deoptimization, hobbles the virus so it can be shown to the immune system without making the body sick.

“You could imagine reading a text … and every letter is a different font, or every letter is a different size, then the text is much harder to read. And this is basically what we do in codon pair deoptimization,” Wyler said.

In the hamster studies, which were published Monday in the journal Nature Microbiology, two doses of the live but weakened nasal vaccine created a much stronger immune response than either two doses of an mRNA-based vaccine or one that uses an adenovirus to ferry the vaccine instructions into cells.

The researchers think the live weakened vaccine probably worked better because it closely mimics the process of a natural infection.

The nasal vaccine also previews the entire coronavirus for the body, not just its spike proteins like current Covid-19 vaccines do, so the hamsters were able to make immune weapons against a wider range of targets.

As promising as all this sounds, vaccine experts say caution is warranted. This vaccine still has to pass more tests before it’s ready for use, but they say the results look encouraging.

Health officials consider another round of bivalent boosters for the most vulnerable Americans.

“They did a very nice job. This is obviously a competent and thoughtful team that did this work, and impressive in the scope of what they did. Now it just needs to be repeated,” perhaps in primates and certainly in humans before it can be widely used, noted Dr. Greg Poland, who designs vaccines at the Mayo Clinic. He was not involved in the fresh research.

The study began in 2021, before the Omicron variant was around, so the vaccine tested in these experiments was made with the original strain of the coronavirus. In the experiments, when they infected animals with Omicron, the live but weakened nasal vaccine still performed better than the others, but its ability to neutralize the virus was diminished. Researchers think it will need an enhancement.

Recent findings suggest that it also needs to be tested in humans, and Wyler indicates they’re working on that. The scientists have partnered with a Swiss manufacturer called RocketVax to start phase I clinical trials.

Other vaccines are further along, but the progress has been “slow and halting,” Poland said. Groups working on these vaccines are struggling to raise the steep costs of getting a latest vaccine to market, and they’re doing it in a setting where people tend to think the vaccine race has been won and done.

According to recent reports, in reality, Poland stated, we’re far from that. All it would take is another Omicron-level shift in the evolution of the virus, and we could be back at square one, with no effective tools against the coronavirus.

Recent findings suggest that “That’s foolish. We should be developing a pan-coronavirus vaccine that does induce mucosal immunity and that is long-lived,” he said.

At least four nasal vaccines for Covid-19 have reached late-stage testing in people, according to the World Health Organization’s vaccine tracker.

The nasal vaccines in use in China and India rely on harmless adenoviruses to ferry their instructions into cells, although effectiveness data for these has not been published.

Two other nasal vaccines are finishing human studies.

Covid vaccine maker Novavax claims it may not survive.

One, a recombinant vaccine that can be produced cheaply in chicken eggs, the same way many flu vaccines are, is being put through its paces by researchers at Mount Sinai in Newly introduced York City.

Another, like the German vaccine, uses a live but weakened version of the virus. It’s being developed by a tech giant called Codagenix. Results of those studies, which were carried out in South America and Africa, may come later this year.

The German team states it’s eagerly watching for the Codagenix data.

“They will be very crucial in order to know where whether this kind of attempt is basically promising or not,” Wyler said.

According to recent reports, they have reason to worry. Respiratory infections have proved to be tough targets for inhaled vaccines.

Industry observers note that fluMist, a live but weakened form of the flu virus, works reasonably well in children but doesn’t help adults as much. The reason is thought to be that adults already have immune memory for the flu, and when the virus is injected into the nose, the vaccine mostly boosts what’s already there.

Still, some of the most potent vaccines such as the vaccine against measles, mumps and rubella use live attenuated viruses, so it’s a promising approach.

Sources indicate that another consideration is that live vaccines can’t be taken by everyone. People with very compromised immunity are often cautioned against using live vaccines because even these very weakened viruses may be risky for them.

“Although it’s strongly attenuated, it’s still a real virus,” Wyler said, so it would have to be used carefully.

Two monster black holes from the dawn of time defy explanation

📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1265 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sciencedaily

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that astronomers have identified an extraordinary pair of quasars dating back to just 900 million years after the Significant Bang.
  • An international research team has discovered the most distant compact pair of quasars ever observed, offering a rare glimpse into the earliest stages of cosmic history.
  • Sources indicate that although astronomers believe paired quasars should be relatively common, finding and studying them is exceptionally difficult.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that astronomers have identified an extraordinary pair of quasars dating back to just 900 million years after the Significant Bang. Each is powered by an enormous black hole that somehow grew to an astonishing size when the Universe was still in its infancy. Scientists have no definitive explanation for how these two cosmic giants became so massive so quickly. The remarkable pair has been given the Hawaiian name Nāpōwawāʻenakaulua.

An international research team has discovered the most distant compact pair of quasars ever observed, offering a rare glimpse into the earliest stages of cosmic history. Officially designated J1602+4228AB and nicknamed Nāpōwawāʻenakaulua, the pair also holds the record for the closest separation between two known quasars from the early period known as cosmic dawn.

Sources indicate that although astronomers believe paired quasars should be relatively common, finding and studying them is exceptionally difficult. Discovering two so close together, especially from such an early period in the Universe's history, makes this finding particularly remarkable.

The discovery was made possible by combining observations from the James Webb Space Telescope (JWST) and the Gemini North telescope on Maunakea, a dormant volcano in Hawai'i. The research was led by Silvia Onorato, a postdoctoral research associate at NSF NOIRLab, and is described in a paper published in The Astrophysical Journal Letters.

Industry observers note that gemini North is one of the two telescopes that make up the International Gemini Observatory. Operated by NSF NOIRLab, the observatory is an international partnership led by the U.S. National Science Foundation, with participation from Canada, Chile, Brazil, Argentina, and the Republic of Korea.

How Giant Black Holes Formed in the Early Universe.

It has been revealed that during the first billion years after the Big Bang, the Universe underwent a period of extraordinary transformation. Vast concentrations of invisible matter, known as dark matter halos, collapsed under gravity. The earliest galaxies began producing stars, while increasingly massive galaxies developed the first supermassive black holes at their centers.

Industry observers note that as galaxies passed near one another, collided, and sometimes merged, enormous quantities of gas and stars became available to feed their central black holes. Some of the material falling toward these black holes released tremendous amounts of energy. This process, known as accretion, could generate radiation so intense that the glowing region surrounding a black hole outshone every star in its host galaxy.

Astronomers call these extraordinarily luminous objects quasars.

According to recent reports, because galaxy encounters and mergers occur frequently throughout the Universe, researchers expect many quasars to exist in pairs separated by distances smaller than the typical diameter of a galaxy. Yet detecting these systems has remained a major challenge.

According to recent reports, one reason is that a supermassive black hole spends only a relatively brief period in its bright "quasar phase." Another is the enormous distance separating ancient quasars from Earth, which makes them appear extremely faint to ground-based telescopes. Even when both objects are visible, their close proximity can make it difficult to distinguish one from the other.

Two Monster Black Holes That Grew Too Significant, Too Fast.

Nāpōwawāʻenakaulua stands out because it is only the third known quasar pair from cosmic dawn. More importantly, its two black holes were already so enormous at such an early stage of cosmic history that existing theories cannot definitively explain their growth.

Industry observers note that the black holes are separated by approximately 18,100 light-years, equivalent to about one-fifth the diameter of the Milky Way. One has an estimated mass of 1.5 billion Suns, while the other weighs approximately 400 million solar masses.

Recent findings suggest that astronomers see the pair as it appeared only 900 million years after the Substantial Bang, when the Universe was still populated by relatively young stars, galaxies, and black holes. Finding two black holes comparable in mass to many present-day supermassive black holes at this early time raises difficult questions about how quickly the first enormous cosmic structures could assemble.

In a recent development, "There is no definitive theoretical explanation for how a single one of these giant quasars exists so early in the age of our Universe, much less two," says Onorato. "We observed Nāpōwawāʻenakaulua at a time when the Universe was only a thirteenth of its age and astonishingly, its supermassive black holes are just as massive as those we see today.".

Sources indicate that the pair's Hawaiian name reflects the extraordinary forces involved. Nāpōwawāʻenakaulua translates to "Two celestial bodies of fathomless powerful darkness in the brilliance of heat reincarnating energy into the Universe.".

The name was developed through the A Hua He Inoa program, a collaboration involving the ʻImiloa Astronomy Center of Hawaiʻi and the University of Hawai'i's Ka Haka ʻUla O Keʻelikōlani (Hawaiian Language College).[1].

How James Webb and Gemini North Revealed the Hidden Pair.

It has been revealed that the discovery began with data collected by the Aether survey, a JWST research program designed to identify and characterize objects from the early Universe. The project is led by Emanuele Paolo Farina, an Associate Scientist at NSF NOIRLab/Gemini.

Sources indicate that using JWST's Near-Infrared Spectrograph Integral Field Unit, the survey assembled observations of 200 quasars. That sample represents approximately 43% of all quasars known from this period of cosmic history.

While visually examining the survey data, researchers noticed something unexpected. A previously identified quasar, J1602+4228A, appeared to have a companion.

Recent findings suggest that to investigate, the team turned to Gemini North's Gemini Near-Infrared Spectrograph (GNIRS). These observations allowed astronomers to distinguish the two quasars individually, providing crucial evidence about the nature of the system.

Industry observers note that obtaining those measurements was an exceptional achievement. The objects are separated by such a small apparent distance, and the companion J1602+4228B is so faint, that resolving them with a telescope on Earth was expected to be nearly impossible.

According to recent reports, fortunately, the researchers benefited from exceptionally favorable observing conditions on Maunakea. Clear skies and unusually sharp atmospheric conditions enabled them to gather the necessary observations in just two nights.

"The sky over Maunakea was so clean and sharp that we managed to collect the data in only two nights," says Onorato.

The team also used Gemini North's Gemini Multi-Object Spectrograph (GMOS) to gather additional information about the system and refine their understanding of the two quasars.[2].

A Latest Clue to the Universe's First Giant Galaxies.

Exactly how Nāpōwawāʻenakaulua formed remains unknown. However, the researchers believe its extraordinary properties could point to an unusually dense concentration of matter in the early Universe.

In such an environment, frequent interactions between young galaxies may have provided enormous supplies of gas, simultaneously accelerating the birth of stars and fueling rapid growth of the black holes at their centers.

If this interpretation is correct, the quasar pair could help scientists understand how the earliest massive galaxies developed alongside their central supermassive black holes.

"Nāpōwawāʻenakaulua is a really unique environment," indicates Onorato. "It's a laboratory for astronomers to study how the very first massive galaxies and their central black holes assembled together through direct galaxy interactions during these early times.".

  • The 78-year-old businessman and U.S.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Former General Motors CEO and Chairman Dan Akerson doesn't mince words when asked about the challenges the automaker faces in finding a successor for GM CEO Mary Barra: "It's going to be tough.".

He should know. The 78-year-old businessman and U.S. Navy veteran helped with his own succession planning and recommended to GM's board in 2013 that Barra replace him as CEO. She has held the top job since Jan. 15, 2014.

Akerson stated Barra will be hard to replace, citing her success and prominence as the first female CEO of any major automaker and the ongoing challenges facing the automotive industry, such as artificial intelligence, vehicle digitalization, and the rise of China and autonomous vehicles.

"It's going to be very, very dynamic," Akerson told CNBC during a phone interview. "It's going to be a substantial change.".

Akerson declined to discuss potential internal candidates such as GM Chief Product Officer Sterling Anderson, CFO Paul Jacobson or President Mark Reuss, but he stated the eventual successor needs to be dynamic and, if from the outside, "adaptable.".

His comments to CNBC follow a Wall Street Journal report on Tuesday that GM is working with an executive search firm to identify possible outside candidates to succeed Barra, in addition to internal prospects. GM declined to comment on the report or Barra's succession.

Akerson, who came to GM as an outsider from The Carlyle Group in 2010, said selecting an outside candidate might be risky if there are already executives within the organization who have similar leadership and technical expertise.

Sources indicate that "Is there anybody in the organization that has that background that you know better day to day over a period of time? You may be taking a risk by bringing in an outsider," he mentioned.

The prospect of an outsider leading GM would be unusual in the auto industry, where major automakers have generally promoted internal CEO candidates, apart from periods of exceptional disruption such as the Great Recession.

Stellantis, BMW, Toyota Motor, Nissan Motor and Hyundai Motor have all appointed internal executives to their CEO positions in recent years.

Barra has remarked several times that her successor and her longevity in the role would be determined by the board.

A notable influence is likely Hewlett Packard veteran Patricia Russo, GM's longest-serving board member who has been on the board since 2009 and leads its CEO succession planning as independent lead director.

GM's CEO succession planning is done "at least annually," according to the company's yearly proxy filing. That process includes Barra providing the board "with recommendations for, and evaluations of, potential CEO successors and discusses developmental intends for these successors," according to the filing.

That is followed by board members engaging "with CEO candidates and senior management talent at Board and committee meetings and other forums to enable directors to personally assess candidates.".

When Akerson was preparing to retire, Barra was among a pool of four candidates — two longtime GM employees and two relative newcomers — who were finalists for CEO in 2013, he remarked.

Akerson stated he put the finalists through an extended evaluation, asking how they viewed GM's strengths and weaknesses, how they would organize the firm, and their willingness to work together, potentially with other CEO candidates who didn't get the job.

Recent findings suggest that akerson remarked the final decision to appoint Barra was done at a day-and-a-half-long board meeting in Washington. The candidate field was narrowed to Barra and former GM executive Dan Ammann, an ex-Wall Street banker who was GM's CFO before leaving the automaker's Cruise unit, reportedly over a disagreement in strategy with Barra, in 2021.

It has been revealed that "Mary's very deserving of all the accolades she's received," Akerson stated. "She's done a terrific job.".

Barra has been leading the automaker for nearly 13 years, which makes her the longest-serving CEO of the automaker since Alfred Sloan retired after a 23-year career as CEO in 1946.

Akerson stated he believes that, like he did, Barra will have major influence in picking her successor. He described that dynamic as integral to continuing her legacy leading the automaker.

Recent findings suggest that "This is important. I think if she doesn't pick the right person, in four or five years from now and things are back in the trough, that will tarnish her history. But I think she'll pick the right one," he remarked.

NASA’s Northrop Grumman CRS-25 Mission Overview

💡 Key Takeaways

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that NASA’s Northrop Grumman Commercial Resupply Services 25 mission, or Northrop Grumman CRS-25, will deliver about 11,000 pounds of science and supplies to the International Space Station. The mission will be the third flight of the organization’s Cygnus XL, the larger, more cargo-capable version of the company’s solar-powered spacecraft.

In a recent development, the Cygnus XL will launch aboard a SpaceX Falcon 9 rocket from the Cape Canaveral Space Force Station in Florida. Following arrival to the station, astronauts aboard the space station will use the Canadarm2 to grapple the spacecraft before ground controllers robotically install it to the Unity module’s Earth-facing port for cargo unloading.

In addition to food, supplies, and equipment for the crew, Cygnus will deliver several newly introduced experiments aimed at improving drug delivery for cancer and osteoarthritis treatment, predicting cancer spread, advancing treatments for muscle loss, improving radiation sensing, and supporting food production for future long-duration missions. This research includes:.

Cardinal Muscle 2.0 uses the microgravity environment to explore potential treatments for muscle loss. Muscle atrophy and strength loss experienced by astronauts after spaceflight share many features with age-related muscle decline on Earth and occur more rapidly in microgravity without exercise. Researchers will use a muscle tissue model to test different Food and Drug Administration-approved drugs used to treat other conditions can be repurposed to prevent or reduce muscle loss.

The DNA Nano B investigation uses microgravity to manufacture tiny, DNA-inspired particles designed to deliver medicine into dense tissues, such as cartilage and solid tumors. Microgravity may enable more uniform particle assembly, helping researchers refine production methods. The results could advance targeted treatments for cancer and osteoarthritis on Earth.

The Active Radiation Environment Sensor (ARES) will test a small radiation monitoring device to support future Artemis program and lunar missions. The system is designed to integrate with spacecraft systems and provide real-time radiation monitoring inside crew living areas. The results could inform radiation monitoring strategies and crew safety measures for future exploration missions.

Sources indicate that encapsulate-1 uses miniature replicas of patients’ tumors to study how cancer cells move, invade surrounding tissues, and potentially spread. Researchers aim to develop a space-based diagnostic tool that could predict cancer progression months or even years in advance, improving early detection and treatment decisions for patients on Earth.

Ohalo III is a new plant growth facility designed to help food crop production on future long-duration missions. The mostly automated system uses innovative water recovery and air exchange technologies to grow a variety of crops. This research could help lead to better food production methods to keep crew healthy and fed on future exploration missions, including those to Mars.

In a recent development, JOining demonstrations IN-Space (JOINS) will mature technologies that allow robotic systems to join materials directly in space. In-space joining could enable large structures to be assembled and integrated after launch rather than being constrained by the size and volume of a launch vehicle. These capabilities may be needed to build and repair large infrastructure, such as structures that will to support future exploration under Moon Base.

Testing technologies in space helps validate their performance in unique environmental conditions, matures their readiness for operational use, reduces technical risk, and builds confidence for future mission applications.

Additional supplies being flown to the space station include:.

To learn more about NASA’s work in low Earth orbit, visit:.

https://www.nasa.gov/international-space-station.

#184915. Inside the Chinese City Where Furniture Dupes Are Made

Inside the Chinese City Where Furniture Dupes Are Made

📅 24 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 23 min read (4649 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: WIRED

⏱️ ~23 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that on the morning of May 31, 2025, Shirley Bekker made an impulsive decision.
  • Two months prior, Bekker had little knowledge of the city of 9 million; she had no idea what hotel to stay at or where to go once she landed.
  • Bekker was in the process of buying her dream one-bedroom apartment in East London and spent weeks obsessively watching home renovation videos on TikTok.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that on the morning of May 31, 2025, Shirley Bekker made an impulsive decision. The then 29-year-old doctor living in London finally pulled the trigger on plane tickets to visit Foshan, in southern China, for a flight later that same day.

Two months prior, Bekker had little knowledge of the city of 9 million; she had no idea what hotel to stay at or where to go once she landed. But Bekker was convinced that six days in Foshan to furnish her apartment—and possibly having all of the furniture shipped back to London—would still be cheaper than getting everything at home. With over 100,000 followers on social media, she also later turned her adventure into content, detailing her finds and their cost.

Bekker was in the process of buying her dream one-bedroom apartment in East London and spent weeks obsessively watching home renovation videos on TikTok. “When I saw that things like a sofa cost thousands of pounds, I was like, ‘OK, I’m convinced now that I’ll probably do something drastic to not have to pay that much,’” she states. Her social media algorithm was already feeding her a radical solution. “Made in China, shit quality?” a Chinese furniture seller noted in videos on Bekker’s TikTok feed. “Grass sofa? Our factory has mass-produced it; UFO table? Our factory has mass-produced it.” Soon, Bekker says, her “entire timeline became Foshan, Foshan, Foshan.” She learned all about China’s furniture capital, which each year exports nearly $10 billion worth of couches and beds and bathroom vanities, and everything else you could possibly need for your home.

In a recent development, bekker is just one of a growing number of people around the world who order furniture directly from factories in Foshan. By either flying to the city—or through WhatsApp, TikTok, AliExpress, or Alibaba—buyers can commission made-to-order pieces. And most importantly, they can purchase dupes.

In 2025, Shirley Bekker flew to China to buy furniture, hoping that even with shipping the cost would be lower than shopping in London.

It has been revealed that duplicates were once primarily the domain of fashion and beauty, but consumers are now seeking out knockoffs of luxury designer furniture that promise the same quality as the original at a much lower cost—even after international shipping rates and tariffs. During the week of April 13, 2025, the number of videos urging Americans to buy directly from Chinese factories soared 250 percent. Tens of thousands of videos had been posted under hashtags like #ChineseFactory, and many of them were about furniture pieces. Some videos garnered millions of views and included contacts of Chinese sellers in the comments.

@gabwithmeg, a working mom in California, claims on TikTok that she saved at least $100,000 by furnishing her entire house directly from China. “It is all Restoration Hardware and Arhaus-style furniture, and I’m going to tell you exactly how I did it,” she promised her followers in January. @gabwithmeg’s post received over 65,000 likes, and the comments are filled with owners clamoring to opt out of the traditional furniture market, if not bragging about having already done so.

It has been revealed that together, they represent a turning tide in furniture shopping for Westerners. If people can buy a couch that looks exactly like the famous Togo for $200 on AliExpress, why would they pay $4,800 for one from Design Within Reach? Sure, Ligne Roset is a legendary brand, famously crafting all its furniture near the French Alps, made by trained artisans using an almost entirely manual process. But not everyone cares about history, owning an original, or the ethics of intellectual property in design. In fact, some furniture buyers, including Bekker, aren’t even aware that some pieces they covet are copies. Bekker feels that designer furniture is more expensive because of the brand name, not necessarily the quality. “Sorry to say, for me, it’s a bit bullshit,” she states. “I’m really not one to buy into the idea that the name of the brand makes it worth the price.”.

Sources indicate that “We’re seeing the beginnings of a revolt against the brandification of everything,” says Christopher Sprigman, a law professor at Latest York University who has studied the knockoff economy. As a consumer, Sprigman expects brands to offer good and consistent quality, but there is a perception that “there’s no real quality control, there’s no real integrity, it’s basically just advertising and driving up costs, creating demand, creating desire without any real substantial benefit that the consumer can feel or taste or see,” Sprigman says.

The videos Bekker saw never explicitly stated how much the furniture in Foshan would cost, but she was confident it would be far less than at the posh showrooms in London. Despite not speaking Chinese, she roamed around the furniture markets in Foshan’s warm and humid air. By the end of the trip, she had furnished her entire apartment for around £7,000 (about $9,200). Everything would go in a 20-foot container, embark from Guangzhou on a freight ship, and arrive at an English port more than two months later. Bekker’s videos attracted millions of views, and fans swarmed to the comments with the same refrain: “I have never been so influenced to go to China.”.

Four million people from over 150 countries visit Foshan’s Louvre every year to shop for furniture.

Everyone who goes to Foshan for furniture makes sure to go to the Louvre.

Industry observers note that in the central part of Foshan, the Louvre claims to be one of the largest furniture shopping malls in China, and likely the whole world. At over 4 million square feet, it’s bigger than its namesake in France, which is the largest museum in the world; 4 million people from over 150 countries and regions visit Foshan’s Louvre every year to shop for furniture. Past the facade—which looks like an outdated convention center with blue-tinted windows and rows of country flags above the entrance—is an opulent atrium with marble columns and gilded moldings.

Industry observers note that the complex was designed to be part of a tourist experience package, with official certification from the Chinese tourism bureau. There’s a shuttle bus from the nearest international airport and a five-star Sofitel hotel for guests. In addition to tourists from the US and Europe, there are ever more shoppers, architects, and traders from the Middle East, Africa, Russia, Central Asia, and South Asia.

The Louvre contains showrooms for over 2,000 Chinese brands and 400 European ones, so there’s something for everyone. As many of these brands construct their furniture in Foshan, it’s the ideal place for a showroom. Italian minimalism is one of the most visible aesthetics here, but you’ll also find styles like Russian imperial, “new Chinese,” and wabi-sabi. In most places, photography is strictly prohibited to “protect original designs.”.

But the Louvre is often just a shopper’s first destination. “Foshan is not actually one furniture market. It’s a district, it’s a city, it’s an ecosystem,” notes Claudia Hofmeister, an Australia-based furniture sourcing agent who has helped clients from around the world buy furniture from Foshan; she has personally traveled there at least six times. While the Louvre is the pinnacle of luxury furniture shopping, Foshan also offers other mid-tier wholesale businesses that are 100 percent Chinese, plus lower-end furniture brands that Hofmeister says she won’t touch. “And there’s a whole lot of other models like big supercenters just dedicated to lighting, tiles, and building supplies,” she says.

Sources indicate that for many travelers, the real shopping doesn’t happen there. The dupe factories, along with home construction and decor manufacturers, are a few miles away in Longjiang. Longjiang is known as the hub of furniture manufacturing, where you can find everything from fabrics to timber to metal parts. Its streets are lined with miles of furniture shops and nothing else. The town has its own exhibition center, but it stands in stark contrast to the opulent tourism spectacle at the Louvre.

The Louvre International Furniture Exhibition Center contains showrooms for over 2,000 Chinese brands and 400 European ones.

It has been revealed that every March and August, Longjiang hosts its own furniture fair, which attracts small manufacturers, dealers, and domestic buyers from other parts of China. The furniture brands in the district care less about original design and are sometimes explicit about where they draw inspiration. On the facade of a showroom building next to the exhibition center, a billboard-sized banner advertises a “Lawrence sofa,” a popular 2017 design by the famous Italian brand Minotti that can sell for over $10,000. In their booths, some sellers display portraits of a white “art director,” an Italian flag, or plaster sculptures.

It has been revealed that even for Chinese people, the idea of traveling to Foshan to buy furniture instead of placing orders from home is relatively new. As China’s real estate economy slowed over the past decade, the traditional business model of licensed furniture distribution struggled. Factories now have to contend with tariffs and competition from countries where labor can be cheaper. Sourcing companies position themselves to factories as a more direct connection to consumers. Even though buyers pay to travel, they can save “30 percent to 50 percent” while still gaining access to new designs and high-quality products, notes Lin Fangfang, the founder and chairman of Yueanju, one of the earliest and most influential B2C furniture sourcing agents in China.

Yueanju, which was founded in 2016, indicates it has worked closely with the local government to develop the “travel to Foshan” marketing strategy. On the radio nationwide, ads hype shopping for furniture in Foshan, with organized pickups from train stations and airports, as well as customized factory tours based on specific needs and budget. A typical three-day trip costs as little as $170 per person. Agents take care of everything and even provide a cafeteria and nap area with recliners in Yueanju’s office building in Longjiang. “Even though [Longjiang is] only one bridge away, they just won’t come here because they don’t know about us,” Lin says. “[Now], we can accommodate over 200 visitors with no problem on this floor.”.

Services like what Yueanju offers swiftly exploded in popularity, bringing a steady flow of consumers to what had previously been a business-to-business manufacturing hub. They are now working with clients from countries including the US, Russia, Saudi Arabia, and Australia. In March, during Ramadan, the company hosted a group from Saudi Arabia. “They are royals, so their homes are pretty big,” Lin says. The company customized the shopping experience based on their fasting needs, only going out after 3 pm every day to preserve energy.

Recent findings suggest that the modern history of furniture in Foshan started with a dupe. As the lore goes, in the 1970s a man named Li Jungang working at a carpentry factory got his hands on a couch from nearby Hong Kong, then a British colony. While upholstered furniture took off in Europe in the 17th century, traditional chairs in China were still made of hardwood and had no built-in cushioning. By the 1970s in Hong Kong, upholstered, Western-style couches were all the rage. Li cut open the couch, studied interior construction, and is said to have built what is considered the first-ever upholstered sofa in China. Similar stories citing the origin of Foshan’s relatively short history in modern furniture manufacturing are now proudly recorded in local history books, displayed in furniture showrooms, and retold by every entrepreneur in the city.

The Louvre in Foshan contains showrooms for over 2,000 Chinese brands and 400 European ones.

Italian minimalism is one of the most visible aesthetics at the Louvre, but you’ll also find styles like Russian imperial, “upcoming Chinese,” and wabi-sabi.

The rest of the story tracks the rise of manufacturing in China. As the government started embracing the market economy in the late 1970s, China became the locus of offshore manufacturing for the rest of the world. Foshan’s voracious entrepreneurs and artisans saw an opportunity to remake the city—which until then was known more for kung fu and local cuisine—into a manufacturing powerhouse. The city became known for factories that specialized in building materials, home appliances, and furniture. Foshan’s home goods industry grew to include over 7,000 businesses that account for at least one-fifth of the furniture market in China. In 2025, Foshan exported $2.65 billion worth of furniture alone. “If you have a home, you have something made in Foshan,” notes the promotional slogan and industry alliance launched by the local government in 2022.

As the city became a furniture juggernaut, it developed an obsession with Italy and, more specifically, Milan, the capital of 20th-century interior design. At Salone del Mobile, the internationally renowned annual furniture fair showcasing some of the most innovative designs in the world, Foshan factory manufacturers study the latest luxury designs from Italian brands. A smaller number of companies bring their own products to the fair, and local furniture leaders also visit to help promote government collaborations between Foshan and Milan. In 2011, a Chinese newspaper reported that during that year’s furniture fair, Fendi Casa refused to admit Chinese visitors to its showroom. (Salone del Mobile did not respond to a request for comment.).

Industry observers note that some Foshan furniture makers do copy designs from Salone, and they do it fast. The 2026 fair ended on April 26; by May 11, Foshan furniture factories were posting on Chinese social media about mass-producing the Anywhere sofa by Edra, one of the breakout products of the year. “The first domestic latest Anywhere sofa is here,” indicates a Chinese woman in a brightly lit showroom, walking past a sofa that looks identical to the original, on Chinese social media platform Rednote. The account, under the name HY Casa, says it’s a source factory in Foshan that specializes in “high-end Italian minimal made-to-order 1:1 furniture dupes.”.

Sources indicate that to create a truly convincing replica, snapping a few photos in Milan is not enough. Wang Xunyong is the owner of EIBA, a furniture brand in Foshan that produces high-end dupes of Minotti sofas by ordering the original, shipping it back to Foshan, and taking it apart to study its internal structure, just like Li did in the ’70s.

A stack of pocket springs at the EIBA factory.

EIBA is a furniture brand in Foshan that produces high-end sofa dupes.

Recent findings suggest that before the success of EIBA, Wang had a series of failed ventures—restaurants and several other furnishing-related businesses. Eventually, he arrived at a decision: “Instead of doing a hundred mediocre things, it’s better to take one thing to the extreme,” he says in a video posted on his social media account. In 2023, he founded his current organization with a small workshop model, leveraging his past experience in the furniture business. This time, it worked.

Wang’s factory in Longjiang occupies the fourth floor of a pristine white industrial building, where a polished lobby opens into a modest showroom/workshop. Several rows of finished sofas sit near the entrance beneath ceiling spotlights. Wang has a makeshift office area that he shares with his sales staff. Every so often, a Bluetooth speaker linked to his phone announces in a flat robotic voice that someone has made a furniture order online. On the workshop floor, five or six women cut and sew sofa fabric, while several men shape foam, spray adhesive, and stretch upholstery over frames.

Wang has never been to Italy. His understanding of Italian design comes from sofas dismantled inside his factory. The first time Wang cut open an Italian-made sofa, he was struck by its complexity. It wasn’t just layers of materials stacked together, but rather a system with different densities, cutting methods, and structural logic working in harmony. He compares the sofa manufacturing process to making a cake: You can standardize the baking process by using a mold, but a complex curve would sometimes require human hands. For a long time, Wang says, many factories focused only on replicating the look of luxury couches. The proportions and silhouettes of the sofas were similar to the originals, but the internal structure was oversimplified. But that misses the essence of what makes a piece of furniture great.

Lin Qi, a factory worker, cuts paper patterns.

Zeng Xiaofeng, a factory worker, cutting fabric.

Recent findings suggest that this path isn’t cheap. Purchasing original pieces requires significant investment, often eight to 10 times the price of the dupes his factory produces. Once the model is thoroughly studied, efficiency improves. Today, Wang indicates, his team can complete the reproduction of a new design within 45 days. This methodology has allowed his factory to reach annual sales of 20 million yuan (about $3 million). Unlike Minotti, which makes almost every piece of its custom furniture in Meda, Italy, Chinese factories can count on much lower costs for labor and manufacturing.

Recent findings suggest that to outsiders, Wang’s work is ethically dubious, but he is unapologetic. “What we’re trying to do is copy it first and surpass it later,” he says. “Many people look down on copying others, but we ignore those noises. First, we learn their details and craftsmanship. Once you have the financial strength and vision, you’ll be much better equipped to do your own thing.”.

In his view, as long as a product does not carry the original brand’s logo, it cannot be considered “counterfeit and substandard.” On a more practical level, he has developed strategies to reduce legal risk. Based on his understanding of regulations, Wang says, a piece is legally distinct if there are “seven points of difference,” even if that’s as minor as changing a board’s thickness from 3 centimeters to 2.9.

Wang’s rule of seven is a common belief among Chinese manufacturers, but it’s more folklore than law, says Morgan Pietz, managing partner at the Los Angeles office of Merchant & Gould, who has represented both sides of furniture IP lawsuits. “At least under US law, there’s no rule that if you make seven changes, you are good to go,” he says.

But it is difficult to legally claim that someone has knocked off a furniture design, lawyers say. In the US, most plaintiffs in the furniture industry need to go down one of two routes: Either they register patents for each of their products, or they need to demonstrate that a layperson would be able to discern the product’s origin. Both are difficult hurdles to clear. Design patents can cost around $5,000, including attorney costs and a filing fee for one product, and they only last 15 years; to make a “trade dress” claim, a furniture company needs to show that its consumers recognize the design as being from a specific source. In most cases, furniture designs don’t rise to this level of scrutiny. And no matter which route one chooses, bringing the claim to court and enforcing it could cost millions of dollars.

Sometimes there can even be a correlation between the popularity of dupes and the sales of originals, Sprigman says. When studying the luxury fashion knockoff industry in China, he found that buyers of counterfeit handbags can often move on to purchasing the genuine product once they become wealthier. “For some people, you could view dupes as a gateway drug to the traditional thing,” he says.

To Wang, the production of dupes is not only a furniture industry phenomenon but also indicative of how capitalism in China works more broadly. “Many of our industries started from scratch. If you want results as fast as possible, you have to learn from abroad first. Whether it’s equipment, aircraft, artillery, or high-speed rail, haven’t we always followed this same path?”.

International clients select materials at the EIBA furniture factory in Foshan, China.

In a recent development, still, creating dupes is not a business that can scale infinitely. In Wang’s view, the market for copies has become oversaturated, and competitive price wars are eating into profit margins. Foshan brands are now pivoting to original designs, not only out of ethical concerns but also due to market pressure. One day, when he has enough financial capital and experience, he hopes to develop his own designs. And only then will he consider actually traveling to Italy. Not to copy their furniture, but to experience Italian culture and find inspiration.

“You need to truly immerse yourself in that environment to feel what high-end Italian design is really about” he states.

Almost everything in Nikki Brooks’ latest house came from China, which is how she got the nickname “Container Girl.” Brooks, a TikTok influencer in Texas who finds “affordable fashion” for her followers, started looking for furniture for a new home in 2024. In the past two years, she has bought windows, doors, stone countertops, tiles, beds, sofas, and even a golf cart from Chinese manufacturers, enough to fill four shipping containers.

Recent findings suggest that in addition to her 150,000 followers across TikTok, Instagram, and Facebook, Brooks organized a private Facebook group where over 25,000 members discuss how to source “high-quality, cost-effective materials from overseas—especially China.” In the group, people ask each other how to import, while others share photos of their containers arriving in the US or their beautiful homes stuffed with newly introduced purchases. Through affiliate marketing, Brooks also gets commissions from “some” products she recommends, according to her personal website.

“We’ve seen a whole crop of dupe influencers pop up, whose livelihoods are based on helping their audiences find the best deals,” says Sky Canaves, an ecommerce analyst at Emarketer, who spent over a decade reporting on China. According to Canaves, beauty and fashion influencers can take a 10 to 15 percent commission from the sales they encourage; in furniture, which is purchased less frequently, the rate can be around 5 percent, but the cost per item is higher.

While in Foshan, Bekker bought everything she needed for her latest apartment.

She decided to shop room by room.

It has been revealed that A new generation of consumers—who came of age with Shein, Temu, and Amazon—consult TikTok or Pinterest instead of design magazines and often buy things directly through these apps. They rarely go to stores in person, if at all, and value affordability over virality. (See the Walmart Birkins, fake AirPods Max, Temu celebrity look-alikes, and everything else that’s been duped.).

Sources indicate that “I don’t love the term ‘dupe.’ It sounds awfully cute for something that is essentially buying a knockoff, or a counterfeit, or a theft,” indicates Coleman Gutshall, the vice president of strategic operations at Bernhardt Design, which develops high-end furniture with designers. From his perspective, an original piece of furniture is more expensive not because of an outrageous margin; Gutshall says his company pays fair wages for over 1,500 employees in North Carolina and works with up-and-coming designers. Many iconic pieces that are duped today were conceived of by innovative designers 50 or 100 years ago, he says, “and in order to keep that continuing, you’ve got to have this constant pipeline of designers. If they can’t make a living through loyalty and through designing, then their talent is going to waste.”.

Industry observers note that but not everyone in the design industry is anti-dupe. “There is no way I could ever afford an original, newly introduced Togo sofa,” says Lauren Sinclair, an architect in New York. (A real three-seat Togo—the iconic foam-filled modular couch designed by French industrial designer Michel Ducaroy in 1973 and still handmade in France by artisans—sells for about $10,000 today.) In 2022, Sinclair paid a Chinese factory $200, plus another $700 for shipping, to get a sofa that looks just like a Togo but in a custom color and tailored to the exact size of her small New York City living room.

In a recent development, “As an architect, I typically frown on dupes. Amateur Astronomer? Be a Kilonova Catcher!

📅 24 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 2 min read (477 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Nasa

⏱️ ~2 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Neutron stars are the ultra-dense, city-sized leftovers of dead stars.
  • In a recent development, kilonova Catcher connects amateur astronomers around the world into a rapid-response network.
  • The Kilonova Catcher network has more than 150 registered members on several continents.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Neutron stars are the ultra-dense, city-sized leftovers of dead stars. When they collide, they can release a brief flash of light called a kilonova. These immensely powerful events forge much of the universe’s gold, platinum and other heavy elements. Since a kilonova fades within days, astronomers have to find it fast, and no single observatory can watch the whole sky. But if you have a telescope with a camera, or access to one, you can help find and follow these cosmic fireworks as a part of NASA’s Kilonova Catcher project!

In a recent development, kilonova Catcher connects amateur astronomers around the world into a rapid-response network. When gravitational wave detectors or space telescopes send out an alert, volunteers point their own telescopes at the sky to help find and track the fading light. The network also follows up on gamma-ray bursts, the most powerful explosions in the universe, and catches other short-lived cosmic events whenever the opportunity arises.

The Kilonova Catcher network has more than 150 registered members on several continents. Volunteers work side by side with professional astronomers and observatories. They have already contributed to more than 64 official reports shared through NASA’s General Coordinates Network, the system scientists use to share discoveries in real time. Volunteers’ observations have been credited for their contributions by being named authors in peer-reviewed scientific research papers. Kilonova Catcher volunteers also joined NASA’s lunar Impact Flash! project campaign during the Artemis II mission, recording the tiny flashes of light made when meteoroids strike the Moon. The network is getting ready to help follow up thousands of new alerts from NASA’s new Nancy Grace Roman Space Telescope.

Sources indicate that "Here at Kilonova Catcher, by chasing the light from gravitational-wave events, we’re seeing how a single collision reaches across the universe,” remarked Cristina Andrade, Kilonova Catcher head of operations at the Minnesota Institute for Astrophysics. “The observatories that make this possible will produce an unprecedented amount of data. We need more human minds, more people with their eyes on the sky and on the data, both literally and figuratively. And more importantly, we need more people to realize they are capable of great feats of science, regardless of their background.".

Sources indicate that the Kilonova Catcher project is co-led by Andrade and Principal Investigator Dr. Damien Turpin, a researcher at the French Alternative Energies and Atomic Energy Commission (CEA). Damien noted, “I am inspired by the expertise and drive of our amateur astronomers. They are always digging for more information and pushing the limits of their understanding. This science could not be done without their contributions.”.

To register and become a Kilonova Catcher, visit https://kilonovacatcher.in2p3.fr/ or send an email to kilonovacatcher@gmail.com. Anyone who has access to a telescope with a camera can take part!

Use your backyard telescope to spot the most cataclysmic collisions in our Universe!

One terminal command gave my forgotten Android device a desk job

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, my kitchen junk drawer used to hold takeout menus and coupons, but it has since become a storage spot for old tablets or phones.
  • I had an old AllDoCube iPlay 50 mini Pro 8.4-inch tablet that seemed like the perfect candidate.
  • Recent findings suggest that getting PhoneBox up and running on my tablet and PC couldn’t have been simpler.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, my kitchen junk drawer used to hold takeout menus and coupons, but it has since become a storage spot for old tablets or phones. Like me, you probably have a few devices lying around that are perfectly functional but don’t meet your daily driving needs. It’s tucked out of view, living out its life in a drawer until being erased and donated after someone asks why you’re holding onto outdated, unused devices. Thankfully, PhoneBox has a solution. You weren’t hoarding old tech; you were waiting for the proper use.

I had an old AllDoCube iPlay 50 mini Pro 8.4-inch tablet that seemed like the perfect candidate. I bought the tablet second-hand as a possible major-screen gaming and emulation tablet to use with a telescopic control deck, but I promptly found I vastly preferred just using a dedicated device. Since that realization, this decent little unit has lived its life in “the drawer.”.

Recent findings suggest that getting PhoneBox up and running on my tablet and PC couldn’t have been simpler. After making sure that the Android tablet was in developer mode, the process was as easy as plugging the tablet in to my PC via USB and executing a single copied command in my Linux terminal. The script downloaded the PhoneBox 0.9.29 software for my PC, verified the downloaded checksum against the release, and walked me through a few quick Y/N installation questions. The script offers to create a systemd user service, so the desktop agent introduces after initial login, and even asks if you’d like it to install the PhoneBox APK to your connected Android device.

Industry observers note that I already had developer mode initialized on the tablet but had to go back and allow ADB over USB in settings. The total installation time from copying the script from the project website to everything running on my PC and tablet was less than a minute. The app is MIT-licensed, works on Android 5.0 or later, and requires sideloading, since it is not available on the Google Play Store.

Credit: Nick Indge Credit: Nick Indge.

Sources indicate that the installation script also prints its own uninstall script before it finishes. So often these days, getting rid of an unwanted app feels more difficult than installing it, so I appreciate the straightforward approach the developer has implemented.

The first time you fire up PhoneBox, you get live performance and diagnostic information from your PC, along with several pages of optional content that can be tweaked for your local setup to display information that’s pertinent to your uses.

Sources indicate that where PhoneBox really starts to shine is the widget catalog—a collection of free add-ons that can be added as pages to the tablet’s cycling page layouts. There are more general widgets, such as RSS feeds that display news highlights from your chosen sources, or simple displays like timers or world clocks.

Recent findings suggest that I opted for a few different widgets that caught my eye. One let me view my library of installed Steam titles and launch them on my PC with a simple tap of the tablet screen. Another allows me to control smart home entities hosted by my Home Assistant server. I was controlling the lights in my office from my tablet within seconds of adding the widget. It’s brilliant.

Setting up additional widgets is as simple as adding them to the page layout from the PC’s web interface and hitting save. As soon as I updated things from the PC, the connected tablet immediately began reflecting the changes. I haven’t had the chance to test most of the 131 current options in the widget catalog, but the ones I did try were simple to modify and worked on the first try.

Sources indicate that while I didn’t have any major issues with PhoneBox, I did notice a couple of early annoyances along the way. Windows users should be aware that the PC companion app on that OS is currently unsigned, and they should expect a SmartScreen notification when attempting to install the software.

All control settings live in the web interface rather than the phone or tablet you’re connecting. When I first started messing with PhoneBox, I noticed it displayed my weather location as Tallinn. Nothing against the capital of Estonia, but that’s not weather information that does me much good here in the US Midwest. When I went into the widget settings to change the report location, there was nothing to be found. It turns out that you have to change those settings from the general user preferences section rather than within the widget itself. Not a deal-breaker by any means, but a slight hiccup for someone who was newly introduced to the software.

According to recent reports, connecting the Android tablet with my PC over USB was totally painless, but I never got the wireless route to work in my testing. People are meant to generate a QR code from the PhoneBox web interface on their PC and connect it to their device by scanning the code with their phone/tablet. Every time I tried to scan the code from my device’s camera app, the tablet refused. There’s no QR scanner built into the PhoneBox app, so if your camera app won’t cooperate, the documented path dead-ends. USB was my intended route anyway and works great, but if you’re planning a wireless-only setup, be prepared for possible friction. The documented flow needs your device camera to open the pairing link, and mine wasn’t in the mood.

It has been revealed that these minor gripes should be smoothed over before the release of 1.0. The project is early, but it seems to be moving swiftly. I tested and installed PhoneBox version 0.9.29, which was one of several releases pushed to the project’s GitHub in as many days. One item of history worth noting: On November 20, the project published a high-severity security advisory covering versions 0.9.23 and earlier. The vulnerability potentially allowed another app running on the connected Android device to execute commands or receive stored credentials from the host PC. The flaw no longer existed by the time I tested the package in version 0.9.29, but it’s a good reminder that you’re installing something with deep system access and should exercise appropriate caution.

Recent findings suggest that as long as you’re part of the group that has an old phone or tablet lying around somewhere, and these days I expect that most of us are, then it’s an emphatic yes. Repurposing old devices to find new lives is one of the things that keeps me a tech hobbyist. I love finding genuinely useful and practical applications for devices that have been pushed aside by their manufacturers in favor of the latest and greatest in the lineup.

PhoneBox took a tablet that was forgotten in a junk drawer and destined for donation and gave it a latest lease on life. I haven’t spent a single penny, but I now have a useful secondary display on my desk. The tablet is powered via a dedicated USB port on my PC, and only goes to sleep when my main monitor displays do. Go dig through those mystery drawers in your house, because this one is worthwhile.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • The escalating climate crisis is shifting many people’s purchasing patterns and this extends to the $500 billion dollar global beauty industry which is grappling with a range of sustainability challenges across product manufacturing, packaging and disposal.
  • 'Delay means death': We're running out of ways to adapt to the climate crisis, fresh report reveals.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The escalating climate crisis is shifting many people’s purchasing patterns and this extends to the $500 billion dollar global beauty industry which is grappling with a range of sustainability challenges across product manufacturing, packaging and disposal.

'Delay means death': We're running out of ways to adapt to the climate crisis, fresh report reveals. Here are the key takeaways.

Strategy and consulting firm Simon Kucher’s Global Sustainability Study 2021 found 60% of consumers around the world rated sustainability as an notable purchase criterion, and 35% were willing to pay more for sustainable products or services.

This shift in consumer preferences has propelled many beauty brands to set environmental goals: to move away from single-use and virgin plastics, provide recyclable, reusable and refillable packaging and offer more transparency around products’ ingredients so customers can ascertain how “green” their purchase is.

Sources indicate that however, consumers still struggle to understand the sustainability credentials of many products, according to the British Beauty Council. This is because the industry’s clean-up efforts have been inconsistent, and fall short of making a recognizable impact in the absence of collective goal-setting, global strategy and standardized regulations.

Sources indicate that there is no international standard for the beauty industry on how much product ingredient information to share with customers — or how to do so. Brands can set their own rules and goals, giving rise to confusion and “greenwashing,” where sustainability claims are often touted but not substantiated.

Companies often use marketing language like “clean beauty” to make it seem like their products are natural, for example, when they may not actually be organic, sustainable or ethically made.

After rebranding in the West, many beauty companies are still offering to 'whiten' skin elsewhere.

In a recent development, “The term ‘clean beauty’ has become quite dangerous. It’s used to sell more products,” according to British Beauty Council CEO Millie Kendall, who added that such buzzwords are losing traction in the UK as British customers wise up to their shortcomings. “Customers need better marketing information and certification information.”.

In a 2021 report calling on the industry to have “the courage to change” their business practices, the British Beauty Council wrote that, all too often, even natural ingredients involved in manufacturing products give way to “over-consumption, non-regenerative farming practices, pollution, waste and neglect.”.

“The only way out of this is transparency,” Kendall told CNN.

In a recent development, jen Lee, chief impact officer at US-based brand Beautycounter, said she continues to see confusion over ingredients among consumers. (In 2013, the company rolled out and published “The Never List,” which presently cites more than 2,800 chemicals — including heavy metals, parabens and formaldehyde — it claims to never use in its products.).

“Natural vs. synthetic ingredients has been a conversation. People think natural is safer, but it’s not always the case,” Lee explained. “Natural ingredients formulated in the industry can have toxic load. Heavy metals can occur in natural components of the earth.”.

Sources indicate that mother loses peripheral vision from apparent exposure to mercury in beauty creams. Toxic levels in her home put family at risk, say experts.

“We used to be more natural and organic,” added Sasha Plavsic, founder of makeup brand ILIA Beauty. “What was challenging is (that) raw materials were difficult to source or would come in inconsistently or products wouldn’t perform.”.

Most makeup is created and molded at high temperatures, Plavsic explained. Purely organic materials often fall apart in this heat, leading to inconsistent results and subpar product performance. “Not every synthetic is bad,” Plavsic mentioned. “Sometimes, it helps create the best in class formula.”.

The industry’s plastic packaging is a particular sustainability challenge — 95% is thrown away and the vast majority is not recycled, according to the British Beauty Council.

Recent findings suggest that the cosmetics business is the fourth biggest plastic packaging user globally — after food and beverage, industrial packaging and pharmaceuticals — and plastic is about 67% of the industry’s packaging volume, according to Vantage Market Research. Beauty giant L’Oreal used 144,430 metric tons of plastic in its packaging material in 2021, for example, according to the Ellen Macarthur Foundation (EMF). Estee Lauder Companies reported its brands produced 71,600 metric tons of plastic in product packaging that same year.

And only 9% of the global plastic waste is recycled, according to a report from the Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development. The United States only recycles 4% of its plastic waste.

According to recent reports, single-use plastic is wreaking havoc on the planet. Here's what you can do to minimize your impact.

In a recent development, many brands are trying to phase out harmful plastics from their operations and adopt post-consumer recycled (PCR) plastic. (L’Oreal has set a target of 50% PCR plastic usage by 2025, while Estee Lauder is targeting 25% “or more” PCR plastic — but both are far from achieving their targets.).

“Between 60-70 major global brands have made unprecedented progress” in PCR plastic usage across industries, EMF’s Plastic Initiative Lead Sander DeFruyt told CNN. But DeFruyt stressed that PCR plastic must be adopted in conjunction with brands removing single and virgin plastics from their usage cycles to truly make a difference.

According to recent reports, however, PCR plastic is not easy to find — low recycling rates around the world mean there is limited supply. Meanwhile, demand for it is growing demand across industries, DeFruyt stated. This competition hikes up its price, which is already higher than virgin plastic.

Hair care brand FEKKAI claims that it used up to 95% PCR content in its packaging, but pricing and supply issues posed a challenge, forcing it to currently aim for containers and packaging that feature at least 50% PCR in its packaging.

According to recent reports, “PCR plastic is more expensive than stock plastic. The cost is hard and then sourcing it is too,” founder Frédéric Fekkai told CNN. “PCR is close to our heart, but there is a massive demand, so finding recycled plastic is difficult.”.

Industry observers note that beauty retailers plays a pivotal — and under-utilized — role, with control over stocking decisions and supply chains. But many vary when it comes to the standards they set for brands they sell.

Recent findings suggest that “Smaller businesses do more, full stop,” said Jessi Baker, founder of the technology platform Provenance, which helps brands display their sustainability credentials for customers. “They move more nimbly. Some of them are born-good brands — climate friendliness was part of their setup. They don’t need to restructure their entire supply chain. Their culture already has it compared to the larger brands who need to work hard to change.”.

A history of beauty trends -- and the standards that shaped them.

Recent findings suggest that sephora released its “Clean + Planet Positive” initiative in 2021, which labeled products that met its set criteria. (This is separate from the French retailer’s “Clean at Sephora” program, which is right now facing a consumer lawsuit alleging it carries a significant percentage of products understood by customers to be harmful.) Target launched a similar program in 2022, featuring a “Target Zero” icon for both online and in-store offerings that either have reusable, recyclable, compostable or reduced plastic packaging, or feature waterless or concentrated products.

Still, many steps taken by brands and retailers do not even begin to touch on the waste and pollution generated throughout supply chains, manufacturing and shipping, all huge problems for the industry to grapple with.

According to recent reports, the gaps in standardization in the beauty ecosystem can, to some extent, be filled by certifications such as the US-born B Corporation, or B Corp. This accreditation, one of the most well-known in the beauty space, is issued by the non-profit B Lab, which scores a firm on a variety of criteria around ethics and sustainability. However beneficial it may be among eco-conscious consumers, though, it is at the moment completely voluntary for brands to apply for.

Governments and multinationals enforcing regulations and setting a base line for brands to operate from when making sustainability claims would go a long way to making change, many experts and business leaders believe.

Susanne Kaufmann, founder of her namesake beauty brand, says her efforts in Austria would reap better results if more countries around the world had stricter, more uniform garbage disposal laws.

A trash heap 62 meters high reveals the scale of India's climate challenge.

In a recent development, “I package our product in a recyclable material,” Kaufmann remarked. (Her products’ packaging, which is refillable and reusable, is made from 75% recycled plastic — and is 100% recyclable.) If I send this to the US, the garbage is not separated… and it’s not recyclable,” she explained, referring to inconsistencies in recycling laws across the United States.

It has been revealed that and when it comes to ingredients, the European Chemicals Agency lists 2,495 substances banned from use in cosmetic products marketed for sale or use in the bloc. But the US Food and Drug administration only lists 11, making it more challenging for American consumers to find safer, greener options. The Environmental Working Group, a non-profit watchdog, studied lab tests of 51 sunscreen products in 2021 and found that only 35% of products met the EU standard, compared with 94% that passed the US standard.

However, while government can set minimum requirements, Mia Davis, vice president of sustainability and impact at beauty retailer Credo Beauty, states the needle will move in the private sector.

Sustainable ships: The world's most eco-conscious cruises.

“Regulation can raise the floor a bit. A person who doesn’t know about any (sustainability issues) should still be able to walk into a bodega and get clean products… But that’s never going to be what the market can do,” she noted. “Market leadership is key.”.

Recent findings suggest that in the absence of bold regulations or global standards on sustainability practices, this “leadership” — undertaken both by brands and customers in the beauty marketplace — is likely to be the most immediately impactful vector for addressing the industry’s climate shortcomings. It will take continued collective advocacy and initiative to see meaningful climate-conscious change.
